sens: State of physical well-being of the body, absence of disease
Healing, restoration of health
Medical treatment or remedy that soothes
Overall well-being, harmony of body and spirit
H7500.detail:
1. The word denotes the state of health, the physical condition of the body functioning well, without disease or pain. The Bible speaks of it as a blessing: in Proverbs 3:8, the fear of the Lord "will be health to your bones."
2. It also evokes the process of healing, the recovery when one has been ill or injured: what one seeks to achieve when treating an illness.
3. By extension, the word applies to remedies themselves, to the care that restores health: the means used to heal.
4. Health finally refers to a broader well-being, the harmony of body and soul together, not just the absence of symptoms.
H7500.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that speaks of healing, caring, making whole. It is the name that comes from the verb "to heal": it names what happens when one is cared for. Words from the same family describe the work of the physician or healer in the Old Testament.
H7500.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Proverbs 3:8. It fits within the wisdom of the book of Proverbs, where the benefits of the fear of God and respect for His Law are enumerated: a righteous life brings health, prosperity, and longevity. It is a promise linked to obedience and wisdom.
H7500.portee: Health, in this verse, is not just a medical matter: it is one of the blessings that God grants to those who fear Him and live according to His wisdom. It reminds us that God cares about our physical well-being and that our body is not separate from our relationship with Him.

sens: son of Schemaeja, of the tribe of Levi, during the time of the divided monarchy
H7501.detail: Rephael is a Levite mentioned only once in Scripture, in 1 Chronicles 26:7, as the son of Schemaeja and grandson of Obed-Edom. He belongs to a family of valiant Levites and likely served at the temple in Jerusalem during the period when the kingdom of Israel was divided between the north and the south. His name means "God has healed" in Hebrew, reflecting the trust in the providence of the Lord that the Hebrews held in religious onomastics.
H7501.origine: The name Rephael comes from Hebrew and means "God has healed" (from rephah, "to heal," and El, "God"). This type of name composed with the divine name was common among the Levites and expressed a blessing or acknowledgment towards God. The family of Obed-Edom from which Rephael comes was an important lineage among the temple guardians.
H7501.emploi: Rephael appears only once in Scripture, in 1 Chronicles 26:7, where he is listed among the valiant sons of Schemaeja. He is included in the list of Levites descended from Obed-Edom who had received responsibilities as gatekeepers of the temple. His brothers Othni, Obed, Elzabad, Elihu, and Semachiah are listed alongside Rephael as "valiant men," highlighting the importance of this family in the service of the sanctuary.

sens: To unfold, open something making it flat or wide
To set up, install, prepare a space or furniture by placing it
To support, hold something by keeping it taut
H7502.detail:
1. To unfold, open something making it flat or wide: the word describes the action of extending a surface, unfolding or widening it. In Job 41:21, it speaks of a "harrow that he extends over the mire": it refers to a sharp-toothed object that is deployed over the ground.
2. To set up, install, prepare a space or furniture by placing it: this is the idea of preparing something for use, erecting it. In Job 17:13, Job says "I will prepare my bed" — he prepares his bed in the abode of the dead, making it his dwelling.
3. To support, hold something by keeping it taut: the word can also express the idea of maintaining, sustaining. It is a nuance where the action of extending also implies carrying, holding something in place.
H7502.origine: The root רפד comes from a concrete image: that of padding, of a cushion or surface that is thickened and unfolded. It fundamentally expresses the action of making something flat, wide, and welcoming. The simple form (Qal) means "to extend" in a neutral sense, while the intensive form (Piel) adds a nuance of support, of holding: not only does one extend, but one makes stable and comfortable.
H7502.emploi: The word appears three times in the Bible (Job 17:13, Job 41:21, and Song of Solomon 2:5). In the two uses in the book of Job, it retains its primary meaning of "to extend": Job extends his bed (his couch) to inhabit it, and the Leviathan extends a harrow with sharp teeth over the mire. The context of the Song suggests a finer nuance, that of extending gently and supportively. It is a rare but always concrete verb: it never signifies a purely spiritual action, but always a visible physical gesture.
H7502.portee: This word reminds us that our daily acts — setting up a bed, preparing our dwelling, resting — can take on a profound biblical meaning. In Job 17:13, the image of the bed set up in the abode of the dead speaks of our preparations in the face of death and the rest to come: it invites reflection on what awaits us and the importance of rest in God's plan.

sens: To abandon, cease to support or hold something or someone
To become weak, to weaken, lose strength or courage
To relax effort, cease, stop
To be inactive, lazy, negligent
H7503.detail:
1. To abandon or cease to support: it is to let go, stop holding or supporting. God says to Joshua "I will not forsake you" (Joshua 1:5): He promises not to abandon him. It is also to "let someone die" by ceasing to hold them — the angel of the Lord "let the plague cease" (2 Samuel 24:16).
2. To become weak, to weaken: it is to lose one's vigor, moral or physical energy. When the people learn bad news, "all hands become weak" (Isaiah 13:7): fear paralyzes. "The hands" become limp, without spring.
3. To relax effort, to stop: it is to cease an ongoing action. Samuel says to Saul "stop," requesting interruption (1 Samuel 15:16). It is also the idea of "refrain" or relaxation.
4. To be inactive or lazy: one who "stops" their labor or vigilance fails in their duty. Proverbs warns: "he who stops his hand" at the harvest wastes (Proverbs 12:24, implicit in the field of employment).
H7503.origine: The Hebrew verb raph·ah refers to the image of letting go, of "releasing the grip." The root evokes something that relaxes, softens, falls. It is found in other Hebrew words expressing weakness or softness. In Aramaic, similar forms exist. In the Septuagint (Greek translation of the Old Testament), this verb is often rendered by "aniémi" (ἀνίημι), which means "to release" or "to let go."
H7503.emploi: This verb appears 45 times in the Old Testament, mainly in historical narratives (Samuel, Chronicles), the prophets (Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Isaiah), and wisdom literature (Psalms, Proverbs). God "does not forsake" or "will not forsake" His people (Deuteronomy 4:31, Joshua 1:5): it is a major issue of divine faithfulness. The people or warriors "become weak" or have "hands that weaken" in the face of danger (Isaiah 13:7, Ezekiel 7:17). One can also "stop" an action (1 Samuel 15:16) or "release" an effort. The word covers both the passive (being weakened) and the active (to forsake, to let go voluntarily).
H7503.portee: This word reminds us that a believer's assurance rests on God's unwavering faithfulness: He does not "forsake" us (Deuteronomy 31:6, Joshua 1:5). It is a promise of constancy in the face of our doubts. Conversely, the word warns against moral laziness, the relaxation of spiritual effort, or the abandonment of responsibilities. It invites us not to let our hands weaken in trust and action.

sens: Lacking physical strength or vigor
Soft, slack, without firmness
Fainting, losing courage
Lacking strength or resistance when referring to a people or an army
H7504.detail:
1. This word primarily describes physical weakness: trembling hands, weak knees, a body lacking energy. In Isaiah 35:3, the weak are told: "Strengthen the feeble hands," as if their arms were falling from fatigue and exhaustion.
2. It also expresses slackness, softness: it is the state of someone whose inner tension has relaxed, who has lost their spring. Job 4:3 speaks of "feeble hands" — those of someone who has ceased to fight.
3. The word can qualify the ability to fight or resist. In Numbers 13:18, the spies must report whether the people of Canaan are "strong or weak," meaning capable or not of defending their territory.
H7504.origine: The Hebrew root evokes the idea of "to relax," "to let hang." It literally designates something that collapses, that loses its tension. These are the hands that hang limply, the knees that weaken — the image of a body that can no longer stand. The idea is found in related words: one who "relaxes" their grip, one who "loosens" their embrace.
H7504.emploi: This word appears four times in the Old Testament, mainly to describe physical or moral weakening. In Numbers 13:18, it characterizes a militarily weak people. In Job 4:3 and Isaiah 35:3, it speaks of the "feeble hands" of one who suffers, who is discouraged or exhausted — hands that need to be strengthened. The Segond translates it as "feeble" or "weak" depending on the context. The emphasis is always on the lack or loss of vigor, never on a mere insufficiency of size.
H7504.portee: This word speaks to those who feel exhausted or discouraged. The Bible does not hide human weakness; it responds by calling to strengthen the hanging hands, to steady the trembling knees (Isaiah 35:3-4). It is an invitation to seek in God the strength we do not have, and to support those who are weakening around us.

sens: Father of Paltiel, one of the twelve spies sent to scout Canaan
H7505.detail: 1. Raphu is the father of Paltiel, chosen as a representative of the tribe of Benjamin among the twelve men that Moses sends to spy out the land of Canaan (Numbers 13:9). His name appears only once in the Bible, simply to identify the genealogy of his son.
H7505.origine: The name Raphu means "healed" or "one who has been healed," formed from the Hebrew root that evokes healing. The circumstances of his life are unknown, but this name suggests that he experienced divine restoration or deliverance.
H7505.emploi: Raphu is mentioned only once in the entire Bible, in Numbers 13:9, where he is identified as the father of Paltiel. He belongs to the generation of Israelites at the time of the Exodus and the wilderness journey. His name appears in the list of the fathers of the twelve spies, but no details of his personal life are provided.

sens: Man of the tribe of Ephraim during the divided monarchy
H7506.detail: Rephach is a descendant of Ephraim, a distant ancestor of Joshua. He appears only in the genealogy of the tribe of Ephraim in 1 Chronicles 7:25, where he is presented as the son of Beriah and the father of Resheph.
H7506.origine: The name literally means "healing of breath" in Hebrew, composed of two elements evoking restoration and life. His father Beriah and his brothers Sheerah and Resheph are part of the same genealogical line.
H7506.emploi: Rephach appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 7:25. He is included in a genealogy of the clan of Ephraim that traces back to the ancestors of Joshua, and which includes names of city builders like Sheerah. These genealogies served to establish family ties and inheritance rights within the tribes of Israel.

sens: Part of a seat or piece of furniture against which one leans their back
Support, back support
H7507.detail:
1. The backrest is the part of a seat — chair, throne, or palanquin — against which one leans their back. In the Song of Solomon, it evokes royal luxury: the backrest is made of fine gold, while the columns are silver and the seat is purple (Song of Solomon 3:10), suggesting a throne or a magnificently adorned seat.
2. More broadly, this word designates anything that supports and maintains the back — a back support that offers comfort and security, the image of a stable support on which one can rest.
H7507.origine: The Hebrew word רְפִידָה comes from a root that evokes the idea of support and maintenance. It is a specialized term, infrequently used in the Old Testament, that specifically designates this functional part of royal furniture. Its etymology refers to the action of leaning or holding something in place.
H7507.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in the Song of Solomon 3:10, where it describes one of the pieces of the wedding procession. There is a possible link with similar words in other Semitic languages that share the idea of support. The context shows that the backrest is a visible and prestigious element of the furniture, alongside the silver columns and the purple seat, highlighting luxury and elegance.
H7507.portee: This word paints an image of comfort and dignity: the backrest offers support, stability. For the Christian reader, it reminds us that God Himself is our support — the one on whom we can lean without fear. The luxurious image in the Song also invites us to contemplate the beauty and generosity of God towards His people.

sens: Stop in the desert where Israel stopped after leaving Egypt
Place of lack of water and tension
Site of the battle against Amalek
H7508.detail:
1. Rephidim is a station, a stopping place, that the people of Israel passed through in the desert between Egypt and Sinai. The name means "rest" or "places of rest," but the contrast between its name and the events that take place there is striking: far from being a peaceful rest, it is a place of trial and tension (Exodus 17:1).
2. At Rephidim, the people lacked water, which created a major crisis. It is a key moment where Israel complains against Moses and where God brings forth water from the rock to meet the need (Exodus 17:1).
3. It is also the place where Amalek, a nomadic nation of the desert, attacked Israel by surprise. Moses sends Joshua to fight this enemy while he intercedes on the mountain, his hands raised. This battle foreshadows the spiritual struggles of God's people (Exodus 17:8).
H7508.origine: The Hebrew name literally means "rest" or "multiple rests" (from the word רָפָה rapah, which evokes rest or relaxation). The paradox of the name reveals how stopping places in the desert often brought only trials to the people of Israel: it is God Himself who transforms these moments of crisis into opportunities for growth and trust.
H7508.emploi: Rephidim appears five times in the Bible, all in the Pentateuch (Exodus 17 and Numbers 33). In Exodus 17, it is the setting for two major crises: the lack of water and the attack by Amalek. These events reveal both Israel's fragility and God's faithfulness in the face of the challenges of the desert. In Numbers 33, Rephidim is included in the complete itinerary of the forty years in the desert, reminding us that this place is part of the overall story of the exodus and the journey to the promised land.
H7508.portee: Rephidim reminds us that apparent "rest" places often hide calls to grow in faith and trust. The water crises and the enemy attack show that God accompanies us even in the most difficult and unexpected moments. This desert station teaches that trial is never the absence of God, but an opportunity to discover Him more deeply.

sens: Man of the tribe of Judah during the divided monarchy
Descendant of Zerubbabel and David
H7509G.detail: Rephaja is a proper name referring to a man from Judah mentioned only once in the Bible. He appears in the genealogy of David in 1 Chronicles 3:21, where he is the son of Hananiah. This character is part of the lineage of Zerubbabel, who led the return from exile under the Persian king Cyrus.
H7509G.origine: The name Rephaja literally means "healed by Jehovah" or "God heals." It is formed from two elements: rapha (to heal) and Jah (abbreviation of Jehovah). This type of theophoric name, which incorporates the divine name, was common in Israel and expressed trust in God's saving action.
H7509G.emploi: Rephaja is mentioned only once in the Scriptures, in 1 Chronicles 3:21. It is a name that appears in the genealogical list of David's descendants after the Babylonian exile. He is the son of Hananiah and the brother of Pelatiah, Isaiah, Arnan, Obadiah, and Shecaniah. This context suggests that he lived during the period of reconstruction following the exile, probably in the 5th century B.C.

sens: Man of the tribe of Simeon during the divided monarchy
H7509H.detail: Rephaja is a Simeonite chief mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 4:42, where he is listed among the sons of Jischei who led five hundred Simeonites to the mountain of Seir. He is cited alongside his brothers Pelatiah, Neariah, and Uziel.
H7509H.origine: The name Rephaja means "healed by the Lord" (Rephaiah in Hebrew: rephà, to heal, and Yah, the divine name). It is a theophoric name, common in Israel, which expresses trust in the healing and deliverance granted by God. Several biblical figures bore this name across different generations.
H7509H.emploi: Rephaja appears only once in the provided biblical references, in 1 Chronicles 4:42. He is presented as one of the four sons of Jischei and one of the leaders of the Simeonites who, during the divided monarchy (probably under the reign of Hezekiah), led an expedition to the mountain of Seir, likely to expand their tribe's pastures. His role is that of a minor military or tribal leader, with no detailed account of his actions.

sens: Man of the tribe of Issachar
Son of Tola and grandson of Issachar
H7509I.detail:
1. Rephaja is a man of the tribe of Issachar, mentioned in the genealogical register of his people. He belongs to the lineage of the descendants of Issachar and is part of a family of leaders known for their strength and authority (1 Chronicles 7:2).
2. Rephaja is the son of the chief Tola and the grandson of the patriarch Issachar. His brothers — Uzzi, Jeriel, Jachmaï, Jibsam, and Samuel — are also heads of paternal houses, all reputed to be valiant warriors of their time.
H7509I.origine: The name Rephaja comes from Hebrew and means "healed by God" or "that God has healed" (formed from "rapha," to heal, and "Yah," the name of God). This name expresses trust in God's ability to heal His people.
H7509I.emploi: Rephaja appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 7:2, where he is listed among the descendants of Issachar during the reign of King David. He is presented as a head of a paternal house and a valiant man, part of a genealogy that counts about twenty-two thousand six hundred valiant men. This unique mention shows that he is a minor but respected historical figure in the tribal organization of Israel.

sens: Chief of Jerusalem during the time of Nehemiah
H7509J.detail: Rephaja is a man who lived during the reconstruction of Jerusalem after the Babylonian exile. He was the son of Hur and chief of half a district of Jerusalem. According to Nehemiah 3:9, he participated in the repair work of the city's walls.
H7509J.origine: His Hebrew name means "healed by Jehovah" (rephâ = to heal, Yah = God). He bore a name of hope, common among the Israelites of that troubled time.
H7509J.emploi: Rephaja is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 3:9. There, he is presented as a notable of Jerusalem who supervised the reconstruction work of the walls after the return from exile under Nehemiah's leadership, probably in the 5th century B.C.

sens: Descendant of Saul and Benjamin
Member of a royal genealogy of Israel
H7509K.detail: 1. Rephaja is a man of the tribe of Benjamin, son of Binea and grandson of Saul. He appears in the genealogy of Saul reported in 1 Chronicles 9:43, where he is presented as the father of Eleasa and Atsel, thus continuing the royal lineage of the house of Saul. 2. His name means "healed by Jehovah" in Hebrew, suggesting a divine blessing attached to his birth or existence. Rephaja represents a link in the genealogical chain of Saul's descendants after the captivity, showing how God preserved this lineage through generations.
H7509K.origine: The name Rephaja (רְפָיָה) is composed of two Hebrew elements: "rapha" (רָפָא), which means "to heal," and "Yah," a short form of the divine name Jehovah. The name literally means "healed by Jehovah" or "Jehovah has healed" and was a common theophoric name in Israel, expressing gratitude to God for healing or deliverance. This type of name reflects the faith of parents in God's power over life and health.
H7509K.emploi: Rephaja is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 9:43, in the detailed genealogy of Saul after the return from captivity. He is presented as the son of Binea and the father of Eleasa and Atsel, three generations of the house of Saul. This passage is part of a genealogical list that establishes the lineages of the families of Judah and Benjamin returned from exile, showing that despite the fall of the Northern Kingdom and the destruction of the Southern Kingdom, the noble families of Israel survived and their genealogies were preserved.

sens: State of physical or moral weakness
Loss of strength or ability to act
Cowardice, lack of courage
H7510.detail:
1. The word denotes the state of someone or something that loses its strength, that weakens. It is the image of a body collapsing, of hands that can no longer hold or act. In Jeremiah 47:3, at the time of invasion, fathers dare not turn to their children "so" weak are their hands — meaning that fear completely paralyzes them, they have no strength or heart to protect one another.
2. By extension, this can refer to moral weakness, lack of will or resilience. Weakness is not only physical: it is also the inability to stand upright, to react, to defend what matters.
3. The word can evoke cowardice or abandonment of courage in the face of danger or suffering.
H7510.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that refers to the idea of becoming soft, sagging, losing tension. The form of the word, with the suffix -on, makes it an abstract noun that designates this state of slackness. It is the opposite of strength and firmness.
H7510.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Jeremiah 47:3. In this passage, the prophet describes the invasion of the Negev by the Chaldeans: the sound of war horses and chariots is so terrifying that fathers, paralyzed by fear, completely lose their strength and cannot even turn to protect their children. Weakness here denotes this state of total panic, where fear disarms the strongest.
H7510.portee: This word reminds us that fear can paralyze us and take away our strength — even the bravest can be seized with dread in the face of threat. For the believer, it is an invitation not to fear the events of the world, but to seek strength in God, who alone can strengthen us.

sens: to lower oneself by throwing oneself to the ground, to deeply bend
to strike the ground with one's feet, to make noise by trampling
to humble oneself, to submit through a respectful act
H7511.detail:
1. The word primarily describes the physical gesture of one who throws themselves to the ground or bends very low as a sign of respect or submission. It is a movement of the entire body that expresses reverence: one lowers oneself, sometimes striking the ground. In Proverbs 6:3, the one who has fallen into the power of another must "bow down" before them to obtain their grace.
2. The verb also evokes the action of striking, trampling, making noise while walking heavily. In Psalms 68:31, the bulls and calves "bow down" loudly, perhaps striking the ground with their hooves, bringing silver gifts.
3. Figuratively, to bow down means to humble oneself, to recognize one's weakness and implore mercy. It is to abandon all pride to plead with someone for help, as creatures do before the king of the earth.
H7511.origine: The Hebrew verb comes from a root that means "to strike," "to trample," or "to tread." Its basic image is that of a foot striking the ground with force. The Aramaic word of the same family (rephas) carries the same meaning: to tread, to trample, to walk heavily. This root is rooted in the idea of a vigorous gesture of the body that lowers itself.
H7511.emploi: The verb appears twice in the Hebrew Bible, always in the reflexive form (Hithpael), which conveys the meaning of "to bow down oneself." In Psalms 68:31, it describes creatures bowing down before the king with tributes. In Proverbs 6:3, the meaning is more clearly that of humbling oneself and pleading: the one who has lost their freedom must go to their creditor, bow down before them, and plead for release. In both cases, the gesture is an act of voluntary lowering and often an act of submission.
H7511.portee: This word reminds Christians that humility is not a shameful weakness, but a gesture of wisdom and spiritual survival. Proverbs teaches us that one who has fallen into the slavery of sin must bow down before their creditor, that is, abandon their pride to implore grace. It is a call to recognize our weakness and seek the help of the one who can save us.

sens: To walk on something, to crush it underfoot
To destroy, to completely crush what remains
To dominate, to subdue by force
H7512.detail:
1. The word evokes the physical action of walking on something, crushing it underfoot — as one would trample on a soft or fragile substance. The terrible beast of Daniel "ate, broke, and trampled what remained" (Daniel 7:7): after devouring and destroying, it crushes underfoot what still exists.
2. By extension, "to trample" means to annihilate, to reduce to nothing what remained. It is the culmination of destruction: not only is one destroyed, but one crushes, tramples the remains, leaving nothing behind.
3. The meaning can also be figurative: to dominate completely, to subdue by brute force. The beast exerts absolute, crushing domination over all it encounters.
H7512.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root expressing the idea of walking, of placing the foot. The basic image is that of a foot crushing — a brutal, irreversible action. The apocalyptic context of Daniel (visions of the four beasts) gives the word a symbolic significance: it embodies destructive and tyrannical power.
H7512.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Bible, both in Daniel 7 (verses 7 and 19), in the same vision of the four prophetic animals. The fourth animal, the most terrible, is described three times in succession by its actions: it "ate, broke, and trampled what remained." This repetition emphasizes the extreme violence and relentless destructiveness of this beast. The parallelism with "to eat" and "to break" shows that to trample completes the idea of total destruction.
H7512.portee: This word reminds us that brute domination and cruelty, as terrifying as they may seem, are not the final word: they are visions given to Daniel so that he knows that God sees, judges, and triumphs over evil. For the believer, to trample what remains also evokes the call not to let evil crush us, relying on Christ's ultimate victory.

sens: A floating construction made of wood tied together, intended to transport goods on water
A means of maritime transport for the trade of wood and heavy materials
H7513.detail:
1. A raft is an assembly of beams or wood tied together to form a floating platform. It is a simple yet effective device for navigating water and transporting heavy loads. In the biblical context, rafts are notably used for transporting construction wood: in 2 Chronicles 2:16, the cedar rafts from Lebanon are directed by sea to Joppa to supply the temple with precious materials.
2. The raft is a mode of maritime commercial transport, particularly suited for bulky or heavy goods like timber. It allows for the efficient shipping of resources between regions without requiring an expensive or complex ship.
H7513.origine: The Hebrew word rapsopdah literally designates a floating wooden structure. It likely comes from a root that evokes the assembly or binding of beams. It is a specialized term in maritime and commercial vocabulary, infrequent in the Bible, reflecting the ancient practices of exporting cedar from Lebanon, a prestigious wood highly sought after for grand constructions.
H7513.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in 2 Chronicles 2:16, in the context of the construction of the Jerusalem temple. King Solomon asks King Hiram of Tyre to ship cedar wood from Lebanon on rafts to the port of Joppa. This unique usage illustrates a well-attested archaeological practice: the transport of precious resources from Lebanon to neighboring kingdoms was done by floating tied wood, which descended along the Mediterranean coast. The word thus reflects an important economic and geographical reality of the ancient Near East.
H7513.portee: This word evokes Solomon's wisdom in organizing resources and logistics for the grand project of the temple. It also shows how, even for major spiritual enterprises, the Bible does not overlook practical and material details: building God's temple required obtaining the best materials through existing commercial channels. It is a reminder that faith and concrete effectiveness do not oppose each other.

sens: To balance or support oneself by leaning on something or someone
To rely on someone in a relationship of intimacy or trust
H7514.detail:
1. To lean is primarily a physical gesture: to bend one's body on someone or something for support, like leaning on a stick or pressing against a friend (Song of Solomon 8:5, where the woman rises from the desert leaning on her beloved — she clings to him, she rests on him).
2. It is also an image of emotional dependence or intimacy: the one who leans on another trusts them, surrenders to them, and feels emotionally supported. In the Song, this woman does not walk alone — she progresses in life entwined with the one she loves.
H7514.origine: The Hebrew verb raphaq comes from a root that denotes the action of supporting or bearing a weight. This image of physical support naturally extends to moral support and mutual trust. In Hebrew, the concept of leaning on someone often carries the idea of relying on them, resting on them — not passively, but in a relationship where two people mutually support each other.
H7514.emploi: This verb appears only once in biblical Hebrew, in the Song of Solomon 8:5. It is a passage where a young woman rises from the desert leaning on her beloved — an image of a woman advancing in life while clinging to the one she loves, finding in him a support and security. The context is that of marital love and shared intimacy. This unique occurrence is sufficient to show how the word expresses both a physical gesture and the relational dimension it symbolizes.
H7514.portee: For the Christian reader, this word invites meditation on the nature of support: it is never a weakness, but an act of trust and connection. Just as the woman in the Song leans on her beloved to progress, the believer can reflect on how they lean on Christ and on the brothers and sisters who support them in their walk.

sens: To stir the water by walking in it or striking it with feet
To soil or spoil by violent foot contact
To disrupt the peaceful or pure state of something
To show pride or power by trampling
H7515.detail:
1. The primary meaning is very physical: to make the water move by walking in it, to make it turbulent by trampling. In Ezekiel 32:2, Pharaoh disturbs the rivers like a huge creature stirring in the water, raising the waves (‘You stirred their waves’).
2. By extension, it means to spoil something clean or good by brutal contact. In Ezekiel 34:18, the unfaithful shepherds disturb the clear water by trampling it (‘you troubled the rest with your feet’), an image of corruption.
3. The word also evokes moral or spiritual disturbance: a disturbed fountain is one whose water has lost its purity. In Proverbs 25:26, a righteous person who stumbles is compared to a disturbed fountain — they lose their stability and brilliance.
4. The underlying idea includes an act of power or arrogance: to trample is to dominate, to impose one's strength. Pharaoh disturbing the rivers shows his despotic power.
H7515.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning ‘to trample, to tread underfoot’. It evokes the concrete action of walking on something with force, striking or stirring it with the foot. The image is that of the foot sinking, stirring, disturbing. Biblical contexts associate this word with water, cultivated lands, and metaphorically with the order or purity that is destroyed.
H7515.emploi: The verb appears three times in the Hebrew Bible, only in the provided usages. In Ezekiel 32:2, it describes Pharaoh as a crocodile who disturbs the rivers of Egypt by his movement in the water — an image of tyranny and chaos. In Ezekiel 34:18, it denounces the bad shepherds who not only feed on the good pasture and drink the clear water, but insultingly disturb what they do not consume, out of pure pride or contempt. In Proverbs 25:26, it metaphorically qualifies a righteous person who collapses: a disturbed fountain represents the loss of their moral power. The word oscillates between the literal meaning (treading water) and the moral meaning (losing dignity, integrity).
H7515.portee: This word invites us to see that our actions have consequences: to soil, disturb, or destroy what is pure is never trivial. For the believer, it raises the question of integrity: are we like a clear spring, or have we allowed malice, pride, or injustice to disturb us? Ezekiel 34:18 also warns that those who abuse their power — who ‘trample’ others — will be judged: God sees every act of trampling, every gesture of contempt.

sens: Muddy deposit at the bottom of the water
Muddy and troubled material stirred up by agitation
H7516.detail:
1. Mud is the muddy and silty deposit that accumulates at the bottom of stagnant waters or rivers. It is a thick and soft material, composed of earth, mud, and debris. In Isaiah 57:20, mud represents what rises from the bottom when the waters are stirred up.
2. Figuratively, mud denotes anything that is troubled, impure, and repugnant. In the same verse, it symbolizes the inner state of the wicked: their thoughts and desires boil like a restless sea, rejecting the impure and the waste. It is the biblical image of a heart that produces evil.
H7516.origine: The Hebrew word rèphesh comes from a root related to the idea of deposit or residue. It concretely designates the mud and silt that float or rest in the water. It is a term for troubled waters, one that visually describes what emerges from the bottom and disturbs the surface.
H7516.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Isaiah 57:20. In this passage, the prophet contrasts the wicked with the peace of the righteous: while the faithful enjoy rest (Isaiah 57:19-20), the wicked are tormented inside, like a raging sea whose waters constantly project mud and silt. This unique biblical occurrence is rich in symbolic meaning.
H7516.portee: This word evokes for the believer the biblical image of inner turmoil: a heart at odds with God produces agitation and impurity. It reminds us that malice and sin can only produce trouble, while the peace of God calms the soul. It is an invitation to seek peace in Jesus rather than remain agitated by evil.

sens: Building or enclosure where livestock is housed
Place where herd animals live together
H7517.detail:
1. A stable is a building or enclosed space designed to shelter farm animals — cattle, sheep, goats — for the night or during bad weather. In Habakkuk 3:17, the prophet mentions a catastrophe: ‘there will be no cattle in the stables’, meaning that the livestock will have disappeared and these enclosures will remain empty.
2. More broadly, the word refers to all the domestic animals that live in this space: a well-filled stable is a sign of a prosperous farm and a blessing.
H7517.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root related to the idea of ‘to graze’ or ‘to enclose’. It designates the place where animals are gathered for feeding and protection. The agricultural context of ancient Palestine, where herds were a fundamental wealth, explains the importance of this word in biblical language.
H7517.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Habakkuk 3:17. The prophet places it at the heart of a description of total devastation: when God withdraws His blessing, the fields produce nothing, the trees bear no fruit, and the stables empty of all livestock. This image shows that the absence of domestic animals is a sign of ruin and divine judgment, as livestock represented life, food, and wealth for a family.
H7517.portee: The stable in this prophetic context reminds us that our material security — our work, our possessions, our livelihood — entirely depends on God. Habakkuk's vision invites us to maintain faith even when everything collapses around us: it is a lesson in trust in God beyond circumstances.

sens: Fragment, morceau d'une matière précieuse
Unité de métal précieux servant d'offrande ou de tribut
H7518.detail:
1. A piece is a fragment, a portion — here, clearly, of precious metal such as silver or gold. The word refers to a detached part, a distinct unit of material. In Psalms 68:31, it evokes the pieces of silver that the nations bring as an offering or tribute to the God of Israel.
2. More broadly, a piece is a unit of precious metal used as currency, as a gift, or as tribute. It is less a shaped and recognizable object than a raw fragment or ingot, a weighable and countable piece: pieces are accumulated to form wealth or an offering.
H7518.origine: The Hebrew word רַץ (rats) has an uncertain etymology; tradition does not clarify it directly. It appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Psalms 68:31, where it designates an element of tribute or offering. Its exact meaning — piece, bar, ingot — cannot be established with certainty, but the image remains that of a discrete unit of precious material.
H7518.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Psalms 68:31, within a grand vision where peoples and nations come to bow before God and bring Him precious gifts: 'pieces' of silver. The context reveals that this is an act of submission and worship — the nations acknowledge the sovereignty of the God of Israel by offering Him riches. Although the word is rare and its primary meaning somewhat uncertain, it clearly evokes a unit of value, a fragment of precious metal, countable and exchangeable.
H7518.portee: This verse speaks to faith by reminding us that all the wealth of the world — even the nations and their treasures — belongs to God and bows before Him. The 'pieces' of silver symbolize the tribute that the world pays to divine majesty, inviting the believer to recognize that their own possessions are merely held in trust.

sens: Se déplacer rapidement sur ses jambes
Se mouvoir avec vitesse et impétuosité
H7519.detail:
1. To run means to move quickly from one place to another by putting one foot in front of the other, as one naturally does when hurrying or fleeing. It is the basic movement of a runner.
2. Figuratively, to run describes any rapid and impetuous movement, that of a creature or force moving with speed. In Ezekiel 1:14, the heavenly creatures 'ran' in the Temple, going back and forth with the speed of lightning — an image of superhuman mobility and incessant movement.
H7519.origine: The Hebrew verb רָצָא comes from a root that expresses the idea of running, of moving quickly. It is a concrete word that primarily depicts physical action. In biblical Hebrew, it is the natural equivalent of the Greek τρέχω (trecho) in the New Testament, both describing the rapid movement of a body in motion.
H7519.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Bible, in Ezekiel 1:14, where it describes the supernatural movement of the creatures in the prophet's vision. In this apocalyptic context, the verb serves to show the extraordinary speed and agility of these heavenly beings who fulfill God's will. It is not a common verb in the Old Testament, making its use here all the more striking to evoke the constant and unceasing divine activity.
H7519.portee: Running, in Ezekiel's vision, symbolizes the active and relentless obedience of the heavenly creatures who serve God. It is an invitation to see how the heavenly forces move in service to the Lord with perpetual energy, far beyond human fatigue or slowness.

sens: Accept with satisfaction, receive favorably
Take pleasure in, delight in
Find acceptable, approve
Enjoy, benefit from
Pay, fulfill (debt, obligation)
H7521.detail:
1. Accept with satisfaction, receive favorably: this is the central idea of the word. God agrees to an offering when it pleases Him and He receives it with a good heart (Leviticus 1:4: the sacrifice "will be accepted for you"). Jacob asks Esau to agree to his gift, meaning to receive it with kindness (Genesis 33:10).
2. Take pleasure in, delight in: the word expresses the personal feeling of someone who finds something to their liking. The psalmist says that the one who sees a thief "delights" in him, meaning finds pleasure in it (Psalms 50:18).
3. Approve, consider acceptable: the word can simply mean to judge that something is suitable or worthy of being received. The Lord takes "pleasure" in His people, meaning He agrees with them, finds them worthy of love (Psalms 149:4).
4. Enjoy, benefit from: in certain contexts, especially with the land, the word means "to profit from," "to rest in." The land "enjoys" its sabbaths while it remains desolate (Leviticus 26:43).
5. Pay, fulfill: in some rare passages, the word takes on the meaning of repaying or honoring an obligation (Leviticus 26:41 may relate to this, with the idea of repairing, compensating).
H7521.origine: The Hebrew verb ratsa comes from a root that evokes the idea of "to be willing" or "to be pleased." The root can be linked to the image of turning towards someone with approval. The same root is found in other Semitic languages with a similar meaning. The word has significant cultic usage: pleasing offerings to God is a major theme in the law of Leviticus, which shows how central the notion of divine satisfaction was in Israelite piety.
H7521.emploi: The verb ratsa appears 54 times in the Old Testament, especially in Leviticus where it qualifies pleasing sacrifices (more than ten occurrences). It is also found in the Psalms, where it expresses God's pleasure or favor towards His people, and in the wisdom books (Job, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes). The meaning varies slightly: agreeing to an offering (cultic context), taking pleasure in something or someone (affective or relational context), enjoying something (material context). It is used both for a person who agrees to something (Ezekiel 20:41: the Lord receives Israel "as a pleasing aroma") and for God who agrees (Psalms 149:4: "the Lord takes pleasure in His people"). Sometimes it carries a nuance of compensation or payment (Leviticus 26:43).
H7521.portee: This word is crucial for understanding the relationship between God and His people. It shows that God is not indifferent: He has preferences, He agrees or rejects. For the believer, this means that their actions, their offerings, their life matter to God — they can please Him or displease Him. It is also an invitation to ask, like Jacob, for God to accept what is offered to Him. The word reminds us that serving God is not a legalistic mechanism, but a living relationship where the heart matters.

sens: The favor, the kindness that one person grants to another
The approval, the pleasure that something brings
The will, the desire, what one wishes to accomplish
The acceptance of an offering or a prayer by God
H7522.detail:
1. Grace is primarily benevolent favor: when someone looks at us with grace, they grant us their sympathy, kindness, and support. Deuteronomy 33:23 mentions Naphtali as "satisfied with favor" — filled with the Lord's kindness. It is the attitude of the heart that leads to doing good for us, without us having earned it.
2. It is also what pleases, what is agreeable in the eyes: Isaiah 58:5 asks if hypocritical fasting is "acceptable" to the Lord, meaning if it pleases Him. The word then designates the feeling of satisfaction, almost delight, that arises from something beautiful or good.
3. It is the will, the desire, what one chooses to do: "at will" in Psalms 145:16 shows God satisfying "at will" all that lives — He does it willingly, of His own accord, according to His desire for benevolence.
4. Finally, it is acceptance: when God agrees to an offering (Leviticus 1:3, 22:19), it means He accepts it with kindness, that He is pleased with it. It is God's favorable gaze that receives our prayer or our gift.
H7522.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that expresses the idea of wanting, wishing, finding good. This is why it designates both desire (what one wants) and favor (the benevolent attitude of one who wants to do good to us). In Hebrew, grace is not an abstract force: it is primarily the tender gaze and the generous decision of the heart of a person who loves.
H7522.emploi: This word appears 56 times in the Old Testament, especially in the Psalms and Proverbs. In cultic texts (Leviticus), it describes the acceptance of offerings: a "without defect" victim is a grace offering that pleases the Lord. In the Psalms, the people implore God's grace ("Let Your grace be upon us"), knowing that it is the foundation of all blessing. In Proverbs, grace also denotes social favor: a king grants his grace to one he honors. Everywhere, the word expresses a personal relationship where love and kindness are at the heart.
H7522.portee: Grace reveals that God does not treat us according to what we deserve, but according to His goodness. This word teaches us that the relationship with God is not a simple obedience to rules, but a meeting with someone who looks at us with kindness and takes pleasure in blessing us. For the believer, it is an invitation to seek God's favor and to reflect that same grace towards others.

sens: To take someone's life either premeditatedly or accidentally
To murder, to put to death with criminal intent
To strike fatally
To be killed, to be put to death
H7523.detail: 1. The basic meaning is to take the life of a human being, either voluntarily or accidentally. It is the act of causing the death of a person. In Exodus 20:13, the sixth commandment prohibits "killing," encompassing both deliberate murder and, according to Deuteronomy 19:4, involuntary manslaughter ("when he has unintentionally killed his neighbor"). 2. When it involves a deliberate and malicious action, the word takes on the connotation of assassination or criminal murder. This is suggested in 1 Kings 21:19, where Ahab is accused of being a "murderer" for orchestrating the death of Naboth. 3. The word can also describe the act of killing a criminal in retaliation or justice: this is referred to as executing justice on the murderer, as shown by the many laws on blood vengeance in Numbers 35. 4. In the passive voice, the word means to be killed or to be put to death, that is, to undergo this death inflicted by another.
H7523.origine: The Hebrew verb רָצַח (ratsach) comes from a root expressing the idea of striking or taking life. It is a specific verb for human murder, distinct from other Hebrew verbs for killing (such as שׁלַח shalakh, "to shoot an arrow," or הָרַג harag, which can apply to animals). The root evokes sudden and fatal action. The word belongs to the legal and moral vocabulary of the Old Testament, particularly in the civil and religious code of Israel.
H7523.emploi: The word appears 40 times in the Old Testament, mostly in legal and historical passages. It is very frequent in Exodus 20, Deuteronomy 19, and Numbers 35, where the Law establishes a crucial distinction: involuntary manslaughter of a neighbor is distinct from deliberate murder (intention changes everything). The cities of refuge are instituted precisely to protect the involuntary murderer from blood vengeance, while the deliberate murderer "shall be put to death" (Numbers 35:18-21). The word also appears in moral accusations: King Ahab is labeled a "murderer" (1 Kings 21:19), and the prophet Hosea reproaches Israel for falling into murder (Hosea 4:2, 6:9). Job and the Psalms use it to describe the crimes of the wicked.
H7523.portee: This verb lays the biblical foundation for the absolute value of human life. The prohibition against murder is not aimed at protecting property or objects, but a person created in the image of God. The text also shows that God's Law dissociates involuntary murder from deliberate murder: this reveals that God looks at the intention of the heart and judges according to justice, not according to raw outcome. For the Christian, this commandment invites respect for life as a gift from God and to examine one's heart in the face of anger and hostility.

sens: To break, to reduce something solid into shards
To destroy violently and brutally
To cause a rupture, an inner destruction (figuratively)
Carnage, massive destruction in a conflict
H7524.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes the action of breaking, reducing something solid into pieces — the image is that of a violent force that breaks or crushes. In Ezekiel 21:27, there is mention of raising up rams (siege machines) and commanding the carnage, referring to brutal destruction by war.
2. The meaning broadens: it refers to total destruction, the annihilation that accompanies the fighting or siege of a city. The order is given to the besiegers to shatter, that is, to launch the final and deadly assault.
3. In the psalmist's context, the word takes on an inner dimension: "My bones are shattered" (Psalms 42:11) expresses not a physical injury, but a deep distress, a rupture of the soul in the face of persecution and doubt — the image of the body disintegrating symbolizes inner dislocation.
4. By extension, the term can also refer to the very result: the carnage, the destruction of human lives in the slaughter of battle.
H7524.origine: This Hebrew word comes from the root that carries the idea of breaking, shattering. The initial image is that of a force that reduces something solid, whole, into fragments. It is found in contexts of physical violence (the rams that shatter walls) or moral (the soul that breaks).
H7524.emploi: The word appears twice in the Hebrew Bible. First in Psalms 42:11, in a context of personal lament: the psalmist, persecuted, feels his bones shatter, a poetic image of inner dislocation in the face of doubt and mockery. Then in Ezekiel 21:27, during the prophecy against Jerusalem: it refers to military carnage, the order given to the besiegers to trigger the total destruction of the city. The word thus shifts from the literal sense (physically breaking) to the sense of disaster, whether human or internal.
H7524.portee: This word reminds us that rupture can be physical, but also internal — the soul can shatter under the weight of doubt and persecution, just as walls under the blows of the ram. For the believer in distress, it names the experience of disintegration, while inviting to still seek God in the very heart of this rupture (Psalms 42:11: "Why are you cast down, O my soul?").

sens: A man from the tribe of Asher during the time of the divided monarchy
H7525.detail: Ritsja is a man from the tribe of Asher, a descendant of Ulla. He appears in the genealogy of the Asherites in 1 Chronicles 7:39, where he is mentioned as the brother of Arach and Hanniel. This character does not appear elsewhere in the Bible.
H7525.origine: The name Ritsja (means "delight" or "pleasure") belongs to the class of Hebrew names expressing satisfaction or joy. It is formed from a root that evokes what is pleasant and good. This name is specific to this character in the Asherite genealogy.
H7525.emploi: Ritsja appears only once in the entire Bible, in 1 Chronicles 7:39. He is mentioned in the genealogical record of the tribe of Asher, in the lineage of Ulla, alongside his brothers Arach and Hanniel. This genealogical context, drawn up after the exile, documents the ancient tribal lineages of Israel without providing further details about his life or role.

sens: King of Damascus during the time of Ahaz and Jotham, kings of Judah
Leader of a coalition against Jerusalem
Enemy defeated by the king of Assyria
H7526G.detail:
1. Rezin is a king of Syria (Damascus) who reigns during the period of the divided kingdoms of Israel and Judah. He is first mentioned during the reign of King Jotham of Judah (2 Kings 15:37).
2. He leads a military coalition with Pekah, king of Israel, to attack Jerusalem and Ahaz, the king of Judah who succeeded him. Although Rezin besieges the city and captures Elath, he fails to defeat Ahaz (2 Kings 16:5-6).
3. The king of Assyria intervenes at the request of Ahaz, marches against Damascus, captures the city, and kills Rezin (2 Kings 16:9), thus ending the Syrian threat to Judah.
H7526G.origine: The name Rezin means "firm" or "he who holds fast" in Hebrew, evoking solidity or determination. It is a proper name without a directly related Hebrew family in the biblical text.
H7526G.emploi: Rezin appears nine times in the Bible, almost exclusively in the historical accounts of 2 Kings 15-16 and in the prophetic oracles of Isaiah 7-9 concerning the reign of Ahaz. The texts of 2 Kings present the military facts: the beginning of his hostility against Judah, his attacks carried out with Pekah, and his final defeat by Assyria. Isaiah mentions him as an example of divine threat against Judah, but also as an illustration of the promise of Emmanuel and God's protection over Ahaz, even though this king does not demonstrate the required faith.

sens: Leader of a family of temple servants who returned from captivity
H7526H.detail: 1. Retsin is the founder of a family of servants attached to the temple in Jerusalem. After the Babylonian exile, his descendants are among those who return with Zerubbabel to rebuild the temple and the city. He is a humble yet important figure in the history of the return: he embodies the continuity of worship and the people of God despite destruction and captivity (Ezra 2:48 and Nehemiah 7:50, where his family is listed among other groups of temple servants).
H7526H.origine: The name Retsin means "firm" or "steadfast" in Hebrew, an appropriate image for a man whose descendants endured exile and maintained their place in the service of the temple. No specific genealogical link is reported; he is simply mentioned as the head of his household.
H7526H.emploi: Retsin appears twice in the Bible, in the two similar lists of the return from captivity: Ezra 2:48 and Nehemiah 7:50. These two passages list the families of temple servants who returned from Babylon with Zerubbabel and the governor Nehemiah. Retsin has no other mention in the Scriptures; nothing is known about his personal life or deeds. His importance lies solely in the fact that he was the head of a household of servants whose genealogy has been preserved.

sens: To make a hole in something with a sharp instrument
To pierce a person's ear
H7527.detail:
1. The verb literally means to make a hole or opening by driving a sharp object — like a punch — through a surface. It is the action of piercing.
2. In Exodus 21:6, it specifically applies to the piercing of a slave's ear. The master, as a sign of voluntary and permanent servitude, pierces the ear of the one who refuses his freedom at the year of Jubilee. This is a legal act and attested in ancient law: the hole in the ear visibly marks the commitment to serve for life.
H7527.origine: The Hebrew verb רָצַע comes from a root that expresses the action of piercing or penetrating. It describes the movement of the sharp instrument that passes through the material. The root evokes the image of a sudden and precise action, that of the tool that penetrates.
H7527.emploi: The word appears only once in the Old Testament, in Exodus 21:6. It is found in the covenant code, which regulates the rights and duties of Hebrew slaves. The slave who loves his master and refuses his release at the year of Jubilee presents himself at the door of the sanctuary. The master then pierces his ear with an awl: this legal and public gesture seals his decision to serve perpetually. It is a solemn moment in Israel's civil law.
H7527.portee: This passage reveals how God frames even slavery through law and humanity. The piercing of the ear is not a punitive mutilation but a sign of freely chosen commitment: the slave chooses to remain because he loves his master. It also anticipates the voluntary servitude of Christ, who commits without constraint out of love. This detail of the Law shows that the visible mark of a heart attached to the one being served speaks powerfully.

sens: Finely executed textile work, ornamental work that enriches a fabric or garment
Delicate and artistic creation, the result of patient and meticulous work
H7528.detail: 1. The word refers to an ornate and carefully executed textile work, where colored threads are interwoven or woven according to a precise pattern to create a beautiful decoration. In Song of Solomon 3:10, it is the work of love by the daughters of Jerusalem who adorn the seat of King Solomon: this evokes a creation that only a patient and loving hand can produce. 2. By extension, the word applies to anything shaped with delicacy and art — a harmonious and well-crafted composition. The image suggests not only visible beauty but also the benevolent intention of the one who created it, like a gift of love offered with care.
H7528.origine: The Hebrew root צפף (tsaph) means to adjust, assemble, put together in order. The word רָצַף (ratsaph) is a form of it and retains this idea of assembly and organized arrangement. The basic image is that of scattered elements being gathered and ordered according to a plan: just as embroidery assembles threads according to a thoughtful pattern, the verb evokes this work of composition and harmony.
H7528.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible: in Song of Solomon 3:10, where it qualifies the ornament of King Solomon's seat. The context is that of marriage and celebration, a poetic scene where the young women of Jerusalem have prepared this magnificent seat. The word is positioned as a collective work of love and beauty, emphasizing not only the aesthetic aspect but also the affection and dedication of those who created it.
H7528.portee: This word reminds us that authentic beauty arises from meticulous work and sincere intention. For the believer, it evokes how God composes our lives with care and wisdom, and how our own work, however humble, can become an act of love towards God and others. It is an invitation to contemplate the divine delicacy in the detail.

sens: Stone or rock heated by fire, intended for cooking food
Glowing coal or ember
H7529.detail:
1. A heated stone is a stone that has been placed in the fire to make it very hot, then used to cook food. This is an ancient method of cooking: food is placed on this hot stone or it is put in contact with dough to cook it. In 1 Kings 19:6, Elijah finds at his bedside "a cake baked on heated stones" — God miraculously provides for his food through this simple and effective means.
2. The word can also refer to the ember or the glowing coal itself, the incandescent material that glows in the fire, an image of intense heat and light.
H7529.origine: The Hebrew word רֶצֶף (rétséph) comes from a root that evokes the idea of burning, glowing. It is close to רִצְפָּה (ritsphah), a variant of the same word. The image is that of the stone or coal made bright red by the heat of the fire — a very concrete image, familiar to the ancients who cooked this way without our modern hearths.
H7529.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Kings 19:6, where it describes the heated stones on which the miraculous cake was baked for Elijah during his flight in the desert. It is a concrete detail of the narrative: it shows how God provides for the sustenance of his prophet in a simple and material way, using an ordinary culinary technique of the time.
H7529.portee: This mention of heated stones reminds us that God cares for the concrete needs of his servants — not only their souls but also their bodies, their hunger, and their physical strength. It invites the reader to see in the simple gestures of daily life manifestations of divine providence.

sens: Ancient city of the Near East
H7530.detail: Retseph is an ancient city of the Near East, conquered by Assyria. It appears in the words of the Assyrian king Sennacherib, who lists before King Hezekiah the cities and peoples that Assyria has defeated and whose gods it has subdued (2 Kings 19:12 and Isaiah 37:12). This enumeration, which also includes Gozan, Haran, and Telassar, serves to intimidate Judah by recalling the military power of Assyria.
H7530.origine: The name Retseph literally means "hot stone" or "burning" in Hebrew, an image that could evoke the desert and inhospitable climate of this region in northeastern Mesopotamia or Syria.
H7530.emploi: Retseph appears only twice in the Bible, always in the same passage: the challenge of Sennacherib stated in 2 Kings 19:12 and reported again in Isaiah 37:12. It is a historical city that the Assyrian king brandishes as an example of his military domination, among other conquered cities. In this context, it symbolizes the impossible resistance of nations against Assyrian power.
H7530.portee: This passage invites the reader to consider how faith in God transcends earthly power. Although Retseph has become a monument of Assyrian conquest, the Bible recounts that the God of Israel delivered Judah by miraculously breaking the siege (2 Kings 19:35), showing that the gods of the conquered nations were nothing before the living God.

sens: paved or stone-covered surface
courtyard or paved area of a building
floor of an architectural structure
H7531A.detail: 1. The pavement is a ground surface made of stones or hard materials assembled together. In the temple, the children of Israel "bowed" face down "on the pavement" (2 Chronicles 7:3), which shows a flat and solid surface where one can stand. 2. The pavement often refers to the courtyard or open space of a religious or royal building. The temple has a "pavement" in its outer courtyard "where there were chambers all around" (Ezekiel 40:17), forming a large paved area around which the buildings are organized. 3. The pavement can be made of precious or noble stones. In the palace of King Ahasuerus, "gold and silver couches rested on a pavement of porphyry, marble, mother-of-pearl, and black stones" (Esther 1:6), showing both the solidity and the richness of the covering.
H7531A.origine: The Hebrew word רִצְפָּה (ritspa) comes from a root that evokes the idea of covering or paving a surface. Its original image is that of paving that covers the ground, forming a unified and solid base. This term is particularly used in descriptions of the temple of Jerusalem and royal palaces, where it emphasizes architectural grandeur.
H7531A.emploi: The word רִצְפָּה appears 5 times in the Hebrew Bible, almost exclusively in descriptions of sacred and royal architecture (2 Chronicles, Esther, Ezekiel). In the book of Ezekiel, it appears several times when the prophet describes the courtyards and pavements of the future temple, where the pavement serves as a reference surface for the dimensions and organization of the space (Ezekiel 40:17-18, 42:3). In Esther, it illustrates the splendor of the Persian royal palace. Its use in 2 Chronicles 7:3 emphasizes the concrete place where the community bows before the divine glory.
H7531A.portee: This word reminds us that the worship of the true God is expressed in concrete places built with care — the temple is not an abstraction, but a solid building where the divine presence is manifested. For the believer, the pavement of the temple also symbolizes the stability and solidity of God's dwelling among His people, a sure foundation on which one can stand and bow down.

sens: Piece of burning or glowing coal or stone
Flaming fragment that escapes from a fire
Figuratively: symbol of divine purification or fervor
H7531B.detail: 1. A coal is a piece of coal or stone that burns and glows with intense heat. In Isaiah's vision in the temple, one of the seraphim takes a coal from the altar with tongs and touches the prophet's lips to purify him: it is the living fire, the heart of the fire (Isaiah 6:6). 2. By extension, it can be any fragment of burning material, detached from a source of heat. 3. Spiritually, the coal evokes the divine fire that purifies and transforms: it represents God's sanctifying work on those He calls to service.
H7531B.origine: The Hebrew word ritsphah designates a bright and burning object. It is related to the root that means "to shine" or "to sparkle." The related term retseph (coal) belongs to the same family. The image is that of living fire, both luminous and devastating, which characterizes God's powerful and purifying action.
H7531B.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Isaiah 6:6. It is in the context of Isaiah's transcendent vision in the temple when he is called to be a prophet. The seraphic angel takes the burning coal from the altar of burnt offerings to touch the mouth of the prophet. It is an act of purification and consecration: the divine fire removes Isaiah's impurity and makes him fit to receive and proclaim God's word.
H7531B.portee: This passage teaches that God's call begins with purification. The coal that touches the prophet's lips symbolizes how God removes our guilt and sanctifies us for service. For the Christian reader, this evokes justification and transformation in Christ: it is through His purifying work that we are made capable of bearing His word.

sens: Concubine of King Saul
Mother of Armoni and Mephibosheth
Woman of devotion and courage in the face of grief
H7532.detail:
1. Ritspa is a concubine of King Saul, meaning a woman who lived in the royal palace without having the status of a primary wife. She is the daughter of Aiah, and she first appears in the account of the conflicts between Saul's heirs after his death, when Ish-Bosheth reproaches Abner for having approached his concubine (2 Samuel 3:7).
2. She is the mother of two sons of Saul, Armoni and Mephibosheth, who are mentioned when David seeks to repay a debt to the Gibeonites by delivering descendants of Saul (2 Samuel 21:8).
3. Ritspa primarily appears as a model of fidelity and maternal tenderness: after her sons are executed, she guards their bodies day and night for several months, protecting them from the birds of the air by day and wild beasts by night, until the heavens finally open and rain falls (2 Samuel 21:10). Her silent devotion is so touching that David is informed and moved by it.
H7532.origine: The name Ritspa means "pavement" or "stone slab" in Hebrew, perhaps evoking a solid foundation. No biblical context tells us why she bears this name, but it may symbolize the stability and constancy that her personal story illustrates.
H7532.emploi: Ritspa appears only four times in the Bible, all in the second book of Samuel. She is first presented as one of Saul's women, placing her at the heart of the succession intrigues after the death of Israel's first king. Most of her mentions (2 Samuel 21:8-11) show her at the time when her sons are delivered to the Gibeonites to repay Saul's oath-breaking. It is in these verses that we discover her character: she remains near her sons' corpses, the sole guardian of their honor, throughout the harvest period. This act of a faithful mother, although contrasted with the oath-breaking and violence of the men around her, illustrates human tenderness at the very heart of divine judgment.
H7532.portee: The story of Ritspa teaches the reader that a loving mother can serve God through her daily and silent devotion, even in the face of injustice or misfortune that she cannot change. Her example shows that fidelity and tenderness never go unnoticed in God's eyes and that they have the power to touch the hearts of the mighty themselves, like that of King David. It speaks to us of the price of maternal love and the dignity preserved by remaining faithful to those we love, regardless of the circumstances.

sens: Physically break something or someone with violent force
Severely break or damage an object
Collide violently
Oppress, mistreat someone
Reduce to nothing, annihilate
H7533.detail:
1. The primary meaning is literal: to grind, to reduce to crumbs. When a woman in Judges 9:53 throws a millstone on Abimelech's head, she "crushes" his skull — the blow crushes the bone.
2. The broken object can also simply be damaged or rendered unusable. In 2 Kings 18:21, a "broken" reed cannot support the weight of someone leaning on it.
3. Two bodies can collide violently: in Genesis 25:22, the twins in the womb "jostled" each other.
4. Figuratively, to crush means to oppress, mistreat a man. Samuel asks: "Whom have I oppressed?" (1 Samuel 12:3). In Job 20:19, the one who has "oppressed" the poor will be judged.
5. The term also expresses moral crushing: Egypt, like a broken reed, cannot support those who trust in it, leaving them crushed (Isaiah 36:6).
H7533.origine: The Hebrew root fundamentally means "to grind" or "to crush." The verb can take several forms (simple, passive, intensive) depending on whether one wants to say "to be crushed," "to crush strongly," or "to crush mutually." The initial image is very physical: that of a millstone pulverizing grain.
H7533.emploi: This verb appears eighteen times in biblical Hebrew, mainly in the narratives of the Old Testament and the Psalms. It first describes a violent physical action (breaking a skull, damaging an object). Very quickly, the Bible uses it figuratively to speak of the oppression of the weak: the one who "crushes" the poor acts cruelly (Job 20:19, Amos 4:1). The word also appears in the prophets to describe political collapse: a nation can be "crushed" by its enemies (Judges 10:8, Hosea 5:11). Isaiah uses it more subtly: God will not "break" the bruised reed, nor "snuff out" the smoldering wick (Isaiah 42:3-4), which expresses a form of paradoxical tenderness.
H7533.portee: The word helps the reader grasp the injustice of oppression: to crush someone is a violent act, comparable to grinding stone. The Bible denounces those who "crush" the poor and promises that this evil will be judged. Conversely, Isaiah reveals that God's servant will not "break" the wounded souls — it is a word of comfort for the oppressed.

sens: Who has lost flesh, who is left with skin and bones
So thin as to be ugly or repulsive
Who signals famine or misery
H7534.detail:
1. The word literally describes a living being who has become so thin that the bones are visible under the skin: it is the opposite of a well-fed, fleshy creature. In Pharaoh's dream in Genesis 41:19, seven emaciated cows come up after seven fat cows — a striking image of the contrast between abundance and scarcity.
2. This extreme thinness is not only physical: it is repulsive, unsightly, a deformation of the normal body. The text adds that these cows are "very ugly in appearance" (Genesis 41:19), as if thinness were a form of ugliness. They are so hideous that Pharaoh has never seen anything like them.
3. In the interpretation of the dream (Genesis 41:27), these emaciated cows symbolize the years of famine that will devour the years of abundance — they embody lack, drought, and the threat of death. It is a word that carries the anguish of deprivation.
H7534.origine: The Hebrew word רַק (raq) comes from a root that expresses the idea of thinness and emaciation. In biblical Hebrew, it opposes words that denote fat, flesh, abundance: it is the adjective for lack of substance. The same root can denote what is thin, not thick, empty of content — an idea of depletion that applies to both the body and resources.
H7534.emploi: The word appears only three times in the Bible, all in Genesis 41, in the unique account of Pharaoh's dream. Pharaoh sees seven fat cows devoured by seven emaciated cows (verses 19-20), and Joseph sees it as a sign of seven years of abundance followed by seven years of famine (verse 27). This word does not exist anywhere else in the Old Testament: it is a very rare term, reserved for this symbolic scene. All usages are feminine and plural, describing these enigmatic creatures from the royal dream.
H7534.portee: This word reminds us that thinness and famine are serious biblical realities — not abstractions, but bodies that suffer and lands that dry up. Pharaoh's dream shows how God communicates warning through vivid and memorable images: seven hideous cows represent famine made visible. For the believer, it is a lesson on the importance of foresight and listening: Joseph interprets the dream and saves Egypt (and Jacob's family) from death.

sens: restriction: one thing, no other
limitation: this excepted, besides this
condition: provided that
affirmation: certainly, assuredly
H7535.detail:
1. The word marks a strict restriction: one thing, no other. In Genesis 6:5, "only toward evil" means that all the thoughts of man are toward evil and nothing else.
2. It can also indicate an exception or a limit: "only he shall make restitution" (Exodus 21:19) means "besides this point, nothing else will happen."
3. Placed before a condition, it means "provided that," "as long as": "Give only this land" (Joshua 13:6) expresses a clause of restriction.
4. Finally, with an affirmative phrase, it can reinforce and affirm: "certainly, assuredly," to give weight to what is said.
H7535.origine: This Hebrew word comes from a root that means "to be thin, fine, light." The initial image is that of the rare, the thin, the restricted — hence its meaning of "only, nothing but." It is a very common word in biblical Hebrew, used to express restrictions and nuances in discourse.
H7535.emploi: This word appears 107 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the historical books (Genesis, Exodus, Deuteronomy, Joshua, Kings). Its usage varies according to context: simple restriction ("only the bread"), exception after a negation ("do nothing, except this"), or condition ("provided that"). It adapts to almost all genres of discourse — narrative, legal, divine injunction — and allows the text to add essential nuances to the expressed thought.
H7535.portee: For the reader, this word teaches how God loves to specify His will: not through absolute prohibitions, but often through restrictions and conditions that leave room for human responsibility. It helps to clearly grasp where the limits and exceptions lie in the Law and in divine promises.

sens: Liquid produced by the mouth
Spit, expectoration projected from the mouth as a sign of contempt or outrage
H7536.detail:
1. Saliva is the liquid naturally secreted by the mouth, which serves to moisten and prepare food. Job 7:19 speaks of the time needed to "swallow his saliva," which refers to the simple and physiological act of swallowing in daily life.
2. Spitting is the saliva deliberately projected from the mouth onto someone, an act of extreme humiliation and rejection. In Job 30:10 and Isaiah 50:6, spitting in the face or spitting on someone expresses the most violent contempt: it treats the other as something despicable. Isaiah 50:6 presents the suffering Servant who endures this indignity without resistance.
H7536.origine: The Hebrew word רֹק (roq) simply refers to saliva, the liquid of the mouth. It is a concrete, direct word that does not hide the physical reality. In biblical Hebrew, it can describe either the natural act of salivating or swallowing, or the aggressive act of spitting. The Hebrew verb translated as "spit" in Job 30:10 and Isaiah 50:6 is formed from this same root.
H7536.emploi: The word רֹק appears three times in the Hebrew Bible. In Job 7:19, it refers to the body's natural saliva, a nearly mundane detail of daily life; Job evokes his suffering through the image of a life so unstable that he cannot even take the time to swallow his own saliva. In the other two occurrences (Job 30:10 and Isaiah 50:6), the context becomes dramatic: it shifts from ordinary saliva to spit as a physical insult. Isaiah 50:6, in particular, depicts the passion of the Servant, who accepts the worst humiliations, including being spat upon.
H7536.portee: This simple yet raw word reminds us that in Scripture, even the most trivial details of the human body express misery or indignity. Spitting in the face, in biblical culture, is an unparalleled form of abjection. The presence of this word in Isaiah 50:6, where the suffering Servant endures this shame, invites the reader to measure the humiliation willingly endured for our salvation and the dignity that this suffering confers on the one who consents to it out of love.

sens: to decompose, fall into decomposition
to lose solidity, be eaten away by wear or worms
to wither, gradually disappear
to be forgotten, sink into oblivion
H7537.detail:
1. The verb literally describes the decomposition of organic matter: something decays when it disintegrates and corrupts naturally. This happens to wood exposed to moisture or insects — it loses its substance and becomes unusable. In Isaiah 40:20, the worker chooses wood that "resists" rot, meaning wood that does not decay easily.
2. Figuratively, the word applies to reputation and memory: a name that "falls into decay" is a name that is dishonored, that fades and disappears from collective memory. Proverbs 10:7 contrasts the blessed memory of the righteous with the name of the wicked that "falls into decay" — forgotten, despised, annihilated.
H7537.origine: The Hebrew root רקב (rqb) first evokes the physical image of decomposition and putrefaction. The word belongs to the semantic field of progressive destruction and annihilation. It applies to what loses its integrity, strength, or value — whether it is dead matter or, figuratively, reputation.
H7537.emploi: The verb appears twice in the Hebrew Bible, always in the sense of decay. In Isaiah 40:20, it refers to the vulnerability of wood to natural decomposition — a practical detail in the description of choosing solid wood for an idol. In Proverbs 10:7, the same word is transposed to the moral and memorial domain: the reputation of the wicked "decays," meaning it fades and disappears, while that of the righteous remains in blessing. The physical image of decomposition thus becomes a metaphor for oblivion and dishonor.
H7537.portee: For the Christian, this word invites reflection on what endures and what fades: a life built on injustice leaves a sullied memory, while a righteous life endures in blessing. The image of decay reminds us that only what is founded on truth and justice withstands time and oblivion.

sens: Rot or decomposition of a material, especially bones
Progressive and inevitable destruction, like that of rust or moth
Envy, jealousy, or shame that gnaws at the heart and body
H7538.detail:
1. This Hebrew word first refers to the decay of bones or the rot that eats them from the inside, like a garment that moths devour (Job 13:28). It is an invisible but irreversible destruction that weakens to the point of ruin.
2. By extension, it refers to any destructive force that gnaws: a woman without virtue is to her husband like decay in the bones (Proverbs 12:4), and envy makes the body rot like a disease (Proverbs 14:30). Hosea 5:12 uses it for God's action that will gnaw at Israel like a moth gnaws at fabric.
