3. In Habakkuk 3:16, the word takes on a nuance of physical trembling: in the face of impending judgment, the bones "tremble" and "consume" under the effect of terror. It is the destruction of the body that expresses inner annihilation.
H7538.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of gnawing and progressive destruction. The image is that of an imperceptible but inevitable process: like rust that corrodes metal or a moth that devours fabric, decay silently destroys from within. This is why the Bible uses it to describe moral or emotional ills that slowly weaken: envy, shame, fear of judgment.
H7538.emploi: The word appears 5 times in the Hebrew Bible, always in a figurative sense. In Job 13:28, it describes the decomposition of the body under the effect of time and disease. In Proverbs (12:4 and 14:30), it becomes the image of moral vices: the woman without virtue gnaws at her husband's well-being, envy gnaws at the health of the jealous. In Hosea 5:12, God compares Himself to a gnawing force that will punish Israel. Finally, in Habakkuk 3:16, in the face of the divine theophany, the prophet feels his bones consuming with fear. In all cases, it is always an internal, irreversible destruction, often inevitable.
H7538.portee: This word invites the reader to become aware of the hidden vices that gnaw at a life: jealousy, dishonesty, fear, far from remaining inconsequential feelings, progressively destroy the body and soul. The Bible teaches that virtue and inner peace are precious goods that protect the health of the whole being, while sin, secretly gnawing, will ultimately consume everything.

sens: State of decomposition of organic matter that disintegrates
State of ruin or degradation of any thing
Figuratively: moral or spiritual corruption
H7539.detail: 1. Decay refers to the state of what is rotting, decomposing, or naturally disintegrating — the wood that crumbles, the flesh that corrupts. In Job 41:18, the Leviathan sees bronze as rotten wood: a material that was once hard becomes crumbly, without resistance, almost powdery. 2. By extension, anything in ruin or degraded: a dilapidated object, a building that is slowly collapsing. 3. Decay can also symbolize inner corruption, moral or spiritual degeneration — the idea that something good has rotted from within.
H7539.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root expressing decay and dissolution. It belongs to the family of words describing natural decomposition and ruin. The image is very concrete: it is what disintegrates, crumbles, loses its solidity — like rotten fruit or wood eaten away by time.
H7539.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Job 41:18, where it describes the Leviathan looking at the hardest metals (iron and bronze) as if they were rotten wood — so overwhelming is its strength and power that no material can resist it. The usage underscores complete futility: everything that seemed indestructible becomes soft and crumbly in its eyes.
H7539.portee: This image reminds us that nothing earthly is indestructible, and that even what seems powerful or unchanging can become fragile and useless. For the believer, it invites us not to place our trust in the forces of the world or material wealth, but to seek what is eternal and unshakeable.

sens: To leap, to hop
To move with agility and lightness by bouncing
To dance, to perform dance movements
To stir, to convulse (referring to inanimate beings or animals)
H7540.detail:
1. The primary meaning is literal: to jump, to make repeated leaps. When David sees the ark of the covenant entering the city, he "jumps" while dancing (1 Chronicles 15:29), expressing his joy through jerky and energetic movements.

2. The word can also mean to dance or to perform a dance of joy. In Ecclesiastes 3:4, there is "a time to dance": it is a blessed moment in life when one lets oneself go to dance, the opposite of mourning.

3. Through a beautiful poetic image, jumping describes the movement of animals or even inanimate creatures. Psalm 29:6 says that God "makes the natural elements leap like calves"; the mountains "jump like rams" before the power of the Lord (Psalm 114:4). These images express the divine strength and power that vibrate throughout creation.
H7540.origine: The Hebrew root raqad paints the image of a lively and repeated movement, typical of jumping or leaping. It expresses both the joyful and intentional movement of one who dances and the involuntary movement of what stirs. It is a concrete word rooted in the direct observation of the body in motion.
H7540.emploi: The verb appears about 9 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the Psalms and poetic texts. It primarily describes human actions: David jumps for joy (1 Chronicles 15:29), people dance in times of rejoicing (Ecclesiastes 3:4), children frolic freely (Job 21:11). But poetic usage dominates: the psalmists use "to jump" to describe how nature itself responds to the power of God — mountains, hills, and animals leap as if they are dancing before the Lord. This shift from the literal to the figurative shows the biblical poetry personifying creation.
H7540.portee: This word reminds us that joy before God can be expressed by the whole body, in free and enthusiastic movements. It also invites us to recognize how all of creation, from the greatest to the smallest, vibrates with the presence and power of the Lord. Jumping is not an undignified attitude: it is a natural and beautiful reaction to what is great and good.

sens: Lateral part of the skull, between the eye and the ear
Area of the cheek near the ear
Region of the face that is visible and vulnerable
H7541.detail:
1. The temple is the part of the skull located on the side of the head, between the eye and the ear. It is a delicate area, poorly protected by bone. In the story of Sisera, the stake that Jael drives "into the temple" (Judges 4:21) penetrates directly into this vulnerable region and kills him.
2. The word also refers to the cheek, or more specifically the area of the cheek that extends toward the ear. In the Song of Solomon, "your cheek is like a half of a pomegranate" (Song of Solomon 4:3) evokes this surface of the face, visible and beautiful.
3. It is a region of the face that is both exposed and sensitive, often associated with moments of vulnerability, emotion, or, in the story of Sisera, defense against an attack.
H7541.origine: The Hebrew word רַקָּה (raq.qah) literally designates the fine and smooth area on the side of the head. It is related to the idea of something thin or light. In biblical Hebrew, this term is used to describe a specific anatomical region, with no exact equivalent in a single part of the French body: it covers both the temple and the cheek, depending on the context.
H7541.emploi: The word appears five times in the Hebrew Bible. Three occurrences describe the murder of Sisera by Jael: in Judges 4:21, 4:22, and 5:26, it is the temple that the stake pierces. These three accounts of the same event show how lethal and strategic this blow is. The other two uses are found in the Song of Solomon (4:3 and 6:7), where the beloved's cheek is compared to a half of a pomegranate. Thus, we see the word transition from a vulnerable region in war to a beautiful and desirable area in a declaration of love.
H7541.portee: This word reminds us that the human body is fragile and precious. In the story of Sisera, it shows how a weak woman can triumph over a powerful warrior by targeting a vulnerable point. In the Song of Solomon, it celebrates the beauty of the beloved's face. These two opposing images teach that the body is both a place of strength and weakness, of beauty and mortality.

sens: Location in Israel, in the tribe of Dan
H7542.detail: Rakkon is a small locality mentioned in the distribution of the lands promised to the tribe of Dan. It is located near Joppa (modern Jaffa) and the stream of the Me-Jarkon, a well-irrigated and fertile region near the Mediterranean coast (Joshua 19:46).
H7542.origine: The Hebrew name Rakkon literally means "the temple" or could derive from a root evoking a place of water or spring. This small territory in the land of Canaan has retained this name in biblical texts.
H7542.emploi: Rakkon appears only once in the Bible, in Joshua 19:46, during the enumeration of the cities and territorial boundaries of the tribe of Dan. It is mentioned alongside the Me-Jarkon, suggesting that these two landmarks — the stream and the locality — served to clearly delineate the tribe's possession in this coastal region of northern Canaan.

sens: To mix aromatic ingredients according to a precise recipe
To prepare a fragrant composition as a specialized craft or art
To blend or season elements in an orderly manner
H7543.detail:
1. The primary meaning is that of the technical mixing of aromatic ingredients: it involves combining different spices, resins, and essences according to specific proportions and expertise. In Exodus 30:25 and 30:35, we are described the composition of the holy anointing oil and the perfume of the sanctuary, prepared "according to the art of the perfumer." This is not a simple random mixture, but a precise formulation that requires skill.
2. The word also refers to the person who practices this art: the "perfumer" or the "composer of perfumes." It is a recognized and specialized profession in ancient Israel. In 1 Chronicles 9:30, the sons of the priests who "composed aromatic perfumes" held an important role in the service of the Temple.
3. By extension, the verb applies to any mixture or seasoning prepared with art and intention: for example, the preparation of spices for the funeral of a king (2 Chronicles 16:14), or the symbolic seasoning of a judgment (Ecclesiastes 10:1, Ezekiel 24:10 in the context of preparing for judgment).
H7543.origine: The Hebrew root rakach expresses the idea of mixing, combining distinct elements into a coherent composition. It is related to the notion of art and mastery: mixing haphazardly is possible, but rakach suggests a skilled, measured blend according to rules. The word is used exclusively in areas where precision and expertise matter: the perfumes of worship, the aromatics of royal funerals.
H7543.emploi: The verb appears 8 times in the Old Testament, primarily in the context of preparing Israelite worship. Most occurrences concern the composition of the sacred perfumes of the tabernacle and the Temple (Exodus 30:25, 30:35, 37:29; 1 Chronicles 9:30). It is a reserved art: in Exodus 30:33, "to compose" an oil similar to that of the sanctuary for profane use results in exclusion from Israel, as this composition is so closely tied to holiness. The word also extends to the aromatic preparations of royal funerals (2 Chronicles 16:14), where the honor rendered is manifested by the quality of the perfumes prepared "according to the art of the perfumer." In other symbolic contexts (Ecclesiastes 10:1, Ezekiel 24:10), the verb takes on a figurative meaning.
H7543.portee: This word reminds us that Israelite worship is not improvisation or disorder, but order, precision, and mastery. The composition of sacred perfumes illustrates that the holiness of God requires a thoughtful and loyal approach, never haphazard. For the Christian, this speaks of a commitment that blends right intention, skill, and respect for what is holy.

sens: fragrant and flavorful substance derived from plants
blend of spices and perfumes used for flavoring
that which adds flavor and charm to something
H7544.detail:
1. The word refers to an aromatic plant substance, often imported from the East, used for flavoring and seasoning. In the Song of Songs, the beloved is invited to drink a "spiced" wine — literally "spicy" — meaning a wine to which spices have been added to enhance its aroma and taste (Song of Songs 8:2).
2. The word can also evoke a mixture of perfumes and spices, as was prepared at the time for ceremonies, banquets, or body care. It is the image of something precious, meticulously prepared.
3. Figuratively, the word expresses what makes something pleasant and delightful: the spiced wine symbolizes a relationship made sweet and flavorful through attention and affection.
H7544.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to mix" or "to prepare." It designates the result of this art of mixing: spices and perfumes blended together. It is a rare word in Hebrew, emphasizing artisanal preparation and refinement.
H7544.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in the Song of Songs 8:2. This poetic and romantic context is revealing: the spice here is not merely for culinary or medicinal use, but an act of tenderness and seduction. The spiced wine is a delicate offering, a gesture that transforms the ordinary into the extraordinary. The word refers to the world of delights and Eastern luxury.
H7544.portee: This word invites the reader to perceive how small gestures of attention — the addition of a spice, the choice of a perfume — transform the ordinary into the extraordinary. In the relationship with God, it reminds us that faith is not austere: it can be beautiful, flavorful, delightful. It is an invitation to serve and love with refinement and generosity.

sens: elaborate mixture of several perfumes and aromatic oils
preparation made according to a precise recipe and specialized know-how
sacred ointment or oil intended for divine worship
H7545.detail: 1. The word refers to a carefully prepared mixture where several fragrant ingredients are combined together. In Exodus 30:25, it refers to holy anointing oil, made according to the art of the perfumer: it is not simply perfume poured randomly, but a harmonious and thoughtful composition. 2. This composition requires true expertise and technique: it must be made "according to the art of the perfumer," which implies knowing the proportions, the order of the mixtures, and the right moment. In Exodus 30:35, the perfume is made in the same way, "salty, pure, and holy." 3. These compositions are not trivial: they are reserved for temple service, for the anointing of priests and kings, and for the incense that rises before God. They embody the beauty, purity, and order that worship renders to God.
H7545.origine: The Hebrew word רֹקַח comes from a root meaning "to mix" or "to compose together." It is related to verbs that express the action of forming something by combining distinct elements. The word evokes the idea of a skilled assembly, a deliberate and calculated mixture, as when a perfumer combines different essences to create a new and balanced fragrance.
H7545.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Bible, both in Exodus 30, where God prescribes the formulas for the anointing oil and the sanctuary incense. In Exodus 30:25, it describes the holy anointing oil, made of myrrh, cinnamon, fragrant cane, and cassia, poured into olive oil. In Exodus 30:35, it qualifies the sanctuary incense, composed of pure incense, stacte, fragrant onyx, and galbanum. These two uses show that the word applies to very precise liturgical mixtures, elaborated under divine authority and intended to sanctify the temple service.
H7545.portee: This fragrant composition teaches that the worship rendered to God is not approximate: it requires order, beauty, precision, and obedience to the details of revelation. The fact that God Himself prescribes the exact formula reminds us that holiness is built through faithful conformity to His word, and that every element matters in the construction of a life dedicated to His honor.

sens: artisan who prepares perfumes and ointments
worker specialized in the processing of essences and aromatics
H7546.detail: 1. A perfumer is an artisan who makes perfumes, ointments, and balms by mixing oils, resins, and aromatics. This profession requires specialized knowledge of essences, their properties, and their combinations. In Nehemiah 3:8, during the reconstruction of the walls of Jerusalem, perfumers are mentioned alongside goldsmiths, showing that it was a recognized profession, with its guild of artisans working together for the service of the community.
H7546.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root meaning "to mix" or "to compose." A perfumer is therefore literally one who mixes fragrant substances to make finished products. In the Bible, this term designates a distinct and esteemed profession, comparable to that of a goldsmith or carpenter, practiced by families or guilds of artisans.
H7546.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible: in Nehemiah 3:8, where it refers to the workers who were involved in the reconstruction of the wall of Jerusalem after the exile. These perfumers are listed as an organized professional category, capable of mobilizing its members for collective work. It is a testimony to the existence of specialized trades in the rebuilt Jerusalem.
H7546.portee: The mention of perfumers in the reconstruction of the walls reminds us that every trade, every profession has its place in the building of the believing community. This invites Christians to see their own work, whatever its nature, as a valuable contribution to the common work of God's people.

sens: fragrant substance used for perfuming or anointing
mixture of perfumes, precious oils
H7547.detail:
1. An aromatic substance is a natural substance, often of plant origin, that emits a pleasant odor and sometimes has therapeutic properties. In Isaiah 57:9, the text mentions aromatics alongside oil, showing that they were used to perfume the body, clothing, or places — a gesture of luxury and seduction.
2. The word also designates an elaborate mixture of these precious substances, such as that prepared for kings or for important rituals. It was not a trivial object: accumulating aromatics showed the wealth and importance of the one who possessed them.
H7547.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of "preparation" or "composition." It belongs to the family of words describing the arts of the perfumer and the apothecary — one who mixes and combines ingredients. The aromatic substance thus evokes not only the scent but also the work of the one who creates and prepares these delicate mixtures.
H7547.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Isaiah 57:9. It is used in a context of prophetic reproach: the prophet denounces spiritual infidelity, figuratively represented by carnal seduction where the luxury of aromatics symbolizes the love of earthly pleasures and the distancing from God. This passage shows that the aromatic substance, although precious, can become an image of vanity and idolatry when it diverts the heart from the true God.
H7547.portee: This word reminds us that material riches — even beautiful and pleasant ones — remain fleeting and can mislead us if we seek them in place of God. The passage invites the believer to examine their attachments: do we pursue fleeting pleasures or communion with the Lord?

sens: One who manufactures or sells perfumes and fragrant oils
Craftsman specialized in the preparation of ointments and essences
The profession of a person who works with aromatic oils and resins
H7548.detail:
1. The perfumer is a person whose trade consists of making, preparing, and selling perfumes, fragrant oils, and ointments. In 1 Samuel 8:13, the prophet Samuel lists the trades to which the king of Israel will subject the young women of the people: among them are the "perfumer women," these women skilled in the art of composing aromatic oils and essences intended for worship, medicine, or personal use.
2. This profession requires knowledge of aromatic plants, resins, oils, and their blending. It was a valuable and respected skill in antiquity, particularly in Israel where incense and perfumes played a central role in temple worship and daily life.
H7548.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to compose" or "to mix" fragrant substances. This root is related to the field of the arts of mixing and chemical composition. In Hebrew, the same generic concept applies to one who prepares remedies and sacred ointments.
H7548.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Samuel 8:13. Samuel lists the trades and duties that young Israelites will have to bear under the rule of a human king: he mentions the perfumers alongside the cooks and bakers. This enumeration highlights that the profession of perfumer was a recognized craft and common enough for Samuel to use it as an illustration of the services the king might require.
H7548.portee: This passage reminds us that in God's plan for Israel, human kingship would introduce a centralization of power and a requisition of talents and people for royal interests. The profession of perfumer represents one of the many human skills that would be diverted from their original purposes. For today's believer, this invites reflection on vocation: God gives us talents and gifts, and it is up to us to use them according to His will, not according to human powers that seek to enslave us.

sens: Solid surface that separates the waters
Vault of heaven where the luminaries are placed
Visible space where birds fly
Domain where God's power and glory are manifested
H7549.detail:
1. The expanse is primarily this solid surface that God creates to separate the upper waters from the lower waters (Genesis 1:6). The word evokes something firm, established, that divides and orders.
2. God calls this expanse "heaven" and places the sun, moon, and stars in it to illuminate the earth (Genesis 1:14-15). It is the celestial vault that holds the luminaries.
3. The expanse of heaven is also the space where birds fly, the domain of air and flight (Genesis 1:20).
4. In the Psalms and in Ezekiel, the expanse becomes the place where God's power and glory burst forth: "Praise Him in the expanse, where His power is revealed!" (Psalms 150:1). In the prophet's vision, it supports God's throne itself (Ezekiel 1:23-26).
H7549.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root meaning "to stretch out," "to spread out." It designates what is extended, flattened, deployed — like a solid surface that can be seen and relied upon. The Hebrews conceived of heaven as a firm vault, a stable construction established by God to maintain the order of the cosmos and support the upper waters. It is an image of order and firmness.
H7549.emploi: The word appears 15 times in the Bible, mostly in the early chapters of Genesis and among the prophets. In Genesis 1, it describes the act of creation where God separates the waters by this expanse (6 occurrences). In parallel, God names it "heaven" and fills it with luminaries. In the Psalms (19 and 150), the expanse becomes the theater of divine glory: it recounts the works of God. In Ezekiel, during the vision of the throne, the expanse is the base of God's throne, solid and shining like crystal (1:22-26). The word thus transitions from a cosmic sense (the structure of the created world) to a theological sense (the place of God's manifestation).
H7549.portee: For the believer, the expanse of heaven is not an accident or a product of chance: it is a creation of God, ordered and firm. It speaks of divine wisdom and power. When we lift our eyes to heaven, we see a work of God established to last, revealing His glory. This word reminds us that all order, all stability, comes from God alone.

sens: Very thin, unleavened bread
Food offering prepared for divine worship
H7550.detail:
1. A cake is a very thin, unleavened bread made from fine flour and often soaked or drizzled with oil. It is a flat and light bread, as opposed to thicker cakes. The text of Exodus 29:2 shows how these cakes are prepared: "unleavened cakes drizzled with oil."

2. The cake holds religious significance in Israel's worship: it is part of the offerings presented to the Lord during sacrifices, particularly thank offerings. In Leviticus 2:4, the cake is mentioned among the offerings baked in the oven, always unleavened and with oil. These cakes accompany sacred rituals and symbolize consecration to God.
H7550.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes the idea of fineness and thinness. The cake is bread reduced to its simplest expression: a thin, flat dough that is easy to share. In the biblical context, the absence of leaven carries strong cultic significance, related to purity and separation from the profane.
H7550.emploi: The word "cake" appears 8 times in the Hebrew Bible, exclusively in legislative and ritual texts (Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and once in 1 Chronicles). All occurrences concern offerings of worship. The cake accompanies the consecration sacrifices of the priests (Exodus 29), the meal offerings in worship (Leviticus 2 and 7), and the vow of the Nazarite (Numbers 6). It is always unleavened, often drizzled or kneaded with oil, never used for ordinary food in these texts. It is a strictly liturgical food.
H7550.portee: The cake reminds God's people of the importance of simplicity, purity, and consecration in worship. The systematic absence of leaven underscores the rejection of excess and moral corruption. Offering a cake to the Lord is to present Him the fruit of one's labor stripped of adornments, in authentic humility. This meticulous liturgical detail teaches that God cares about how we approach Him, even in the smallest things.

sens: Mix and intertwine threads of different colors on a fabric
Weave or create a material by interlacing threads
Execute a textile art piece with skill
Symbolically: to be shaped or constructed with care and detail
H7551.detail:
1. To broider primarily means to mix bright threads (blue, purple, crimson, fine white linen) and interlace them on a fabric to form a pattern. It is a task that requires both technique and artistic taste: the curtain at the entrance of the Tabernacle, broidered in blue, purple, and crimson (Exodus 26:36), creates an effect of harmonious and spectacular colors.
2. The verb is used more broadly to refer to the weaving itself, the art of assembling threads on a loom. When Moses commands to "broider and weave the fabrics dyed in blue, purple, and crimson" (Exodus 35:35), he speaks of the complete process of creating textile material.
3. By extension, it means to execute a textile art piece with remarkable competence: the artisans were filled with skill to "broider," meaning they worked with excellence, producing beautiful and durable pieces, like the broidered belt of the high priest (Exodus 28:39).
4. The psalmist uses the word figuratively to evoke divine creation: "I am fearfully and wonderfully made" or "you knitted me together in my mother's womb" (Psalms 139:15) suggests that God formed the human body with attention to detail and incomparable skill, like a precious textile work.
H7551.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that expresses the idea of varying, mixing (hence: colored). It refers to the primary image of working with colors: composing a multicolored material, intertwining different tones. It is not an isolated technical term, but a word from the ancient textile craftsmanship of the Near East, very concrete and very visual.
H7551.emploi: The verb to broider appears 9 times in the Bible, almost exclusively in the account of the Tabernacle (Exodus 26 to 39). It describes the work of divine artisans, notably Oholiab and his companions, who make the curtains and liturgical garments of the sanctuary. These works are all characterized by the mixing of ritual colors (blue, purple, crimson) and the fineness of linen. Only once, in Psalms 139:15, does the verb change domain: it moves out of the artisanal context to become the image of how God formed the human body in the womb. This figurative use enriches the word by giving it a cosmic and theological significance.
H7551.portee: This word reminds the reader that the worship of the Tabernacle was not a primitive and crude worship, but an act of art and beauty, executed by artisans endowed with divine wisdom. It celebrates well-done work, color, harmony — showing that God honors excellence in what concerns Him. Above all, its use in Psalms 139 invites contemplation of the creation of our own body as a divine wonder, composed of a thousand invisible yet precise details, comparable to a textile work broidered from within. It is an invitation to marvel at divine providence.

sens: One of the five kings of Midian at the time of the Exodus and the conquest of the desert
H7552G.detail: 1. Rekem is one of the five kings of Midian who were killed by the Israelites during the vengeance against Midian, after the people committed idolatry at Peor due to the seduction of Midianite women. His name appears alongside Evi, Zur, Hur, and Reba (Numbers 31:8), all five princes of Midian who lived in the land and were subject to King Sihon of the Amorites (Joshua 13:21).
H7552G.origine: The name Rekem means in Hebrew "variegation" or "varied," possibly evoking an ornamentation or distinction. It is a proper name designating a Midianite chief from the Mosaic period.
H7552G.emploi: Rekem is mentioned twice in the Bible: first in Numbers 31:8 where he is listed among the five kings of Midian killed during the vengeful campaign against Midian, and in Joshua 13:21 where he is called a prince of Midian and it is noted that these princes lived in the land and were subject to King Sihon of the Amorites. These two passages are part of the account of Israel's settlement beyond the Jordan and God's divine judgment against the peoples who opposed His plan for His people.

sens: City of Israel located in Benjamin
H7552H.detail: Rekem is a city in the territory of the tribe of Benjamin, mentioned only once in the Bible during the division of the lands among the tribes of Israel after the conquest of Canaan. It appears in the list of cities assigned to Benjamin in Joshua 18:27.
H7552H.origine: The name Rekem literally means "variegation" or "painting in varied colors" in Hebrew, likely evoking patterns or colorations. It is a formation of the verb רקם (raqam), which means "to broider" or "to paint in various colors." The name could denote a visible characteristic of the site or have a lost symbolic meaning.
H7552H.emploi: Rekem appears only once in the Bible: in Joshua 18:27, where it is listed among the cities given to the tribe of Benjamin during the division of the territory of Canaan after the conquest. This mention places it among the localities of the Benjaminite territory at the time of the Israelites' settlement in the promised land.

sens: Son of Hebron, of the tribe of Judah
Father of Shammai
Figure in the genealogy of the divided kingdom
H7552I.detail:
1. Rekem is a man of the tribe of Judah, one of the four sons of Hebron, living at the time of the divided kingdom (1 Chronicles 2:43). He belongs to an important genealogical lineage in the history of Israel.
2. He is the father of Shammai, whose descendants are recorded in the genealogies of God's people (1 Chronicles 2:44). This paternity places him in a chain of family transmission that structures the genealogy of Judah.
H7552I.origine: The name Rekem literally means "variegation" or "bigarrure" in Hebrew, evoking an image of mixed colors or varied patterns. This proper name belongs to the list of descendants of Hebron, whose genealogy reflects the structuring of the tribes during the divided kingdom.
H7552I.emploi: Rekem appears only twice in Scripture, both in 1 Chronicles 2, in verses 43 and 44. He is mentioned only in the context of the genealogies of Judah, where he is first listed among the sons of Hebron (his brothers being Korah, Tappuah, and Shema), and then it is learned that he is the father of Shammai. These occurrences place him exclusively within the genealogical tradition of the chosen people.

sens: Man of the tribe of Manasseh, son of Machir and Maacah
Brother of Sheresh and Ulam
H7552J.detail: Rekem is a man belonging to the tribe of Manasseh, mentioned only once in the Bible. He is presented as the son that Maacah, the wife of Machir, bore and named Rekem (1 Chronicles 7:16). He had brothers: Sheresh and Ulam, all from the same mother. His name means "variegation" or "variety of colors," possibly evoking a distinctive mark or a particularity noticed at his birth.
H7552J.origine: The name Rekem literally means "variegation" or "bigarrure," which suggests a diversity of colors or a varied pattern. This rare name in the Bible appears as a personal name chosen by his mother to mark her child with a visible or symbolic particularity.
H7552J.emploi: Rekem appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 7:16, within the genealogy of the tribe of Manasseh. He is listed as a member of Machir's family, one of the important descendants of Manasseh, during the period of the divided monarchy. His mention, although brief, integrates him into the official lineage of the people of Israel recorded by the chronicler historian.

sens: Needlework made of colored threads forming patterns on a fabric
Richly adorned fabric with embroidered patterns
Luxury garment or fabric, bursting with colors and details
H7553.detail:
1. Embroidery is a needlework where colored threads create designs and patterns on a fabric: it is an art that requires time and skill. In Ezekiel 16:10, God promises Jerusalem "embroidered garments," a symbol of grace and beauty.
2. The word also refers to the fabric itself once decorated — a fabric made rare and precious by its colorful ornaments. In Psalms 45:15, the queen appears "dressed in her embroidered garments," a symbol of royal dignity.
3. More broadly, it is a sign of wealth, luxury, and splendor: embroidered garments are offered as spoils of war (Judges 5:30), and merchant nations consider it a valuable commodity (Ezekiel 27:16-24).
H7553.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes the idea of "variety" and "multicolored." Embroidery itself is an act of artistic creation, a skillful assembly of different colors to form an image or pattern. In Aramaic and neighboring languages, words of the same family retain this sense of what is mixed, varied, multicolored — like an embroidery where a thousand shades meet.
H7553.emploi: The word appears eleven times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the poetic and prophetic books. It refers sometimes to the work (the art of embroidery), sometimes to the finished product (an embroidered garment or fabric). In Ezekiel's visions (chapters 16 and 27), embroidery is a symbol of luxury and seduction: it adorns Jerusalem transformed into a queen, or it is part of the wealth of merchant cities. In ancient times, it was a rare commodity, imported or made by renowned artisans, and thus reserved for great figures. The Hebrew word expresses both the technique and the resulting splendor.
H7553.portee: Embroidery in the Bible is never neutral: it symbolizes beauty, wealth, and the allure of luxury. Ezekiel uses it to show how Jerusalem was adorned with splendor by God, and then how she turned these gifts toward idolatry. For the reader, it is a lesson: the material goods and beauty that God offers can seduce our hearts and lead us away from Him if we forget that everything comes from His grace. Embroidery also reminds us that true beauty is that which God Himself creates.

sens: To flatten and stretch a metal by striking it
To crush, to tread upon
To unfold, to spread outward
To cover or coat a surface
To clap hands in a sign of denial or contempt
H7554.detail:
1. The primary meaning is that of the blacksmith or goldsmith: striking the metal to flatten and stretch it into thin sheets. Exodus 39:3 describes how they "spread out gold sheets" which were then cut into threads to embroider the fabrics of the sanctuary; Numbers 16:39 reports that the priest made "sheets" to cover the altar — hammered and flattened sheets.
2. The word also applies to the action of crushing or treading: in 2 Samuel 22:43, David cries, "I trample them like the mud of the streets," speaking of his enemies crushed under his feet, an image of total victory.
3. By extension, "to spread out" or "to unfold": the image of flattened metal transitions to that of the heavens or the earth that one "spreads out" — Psalms 136:6 sings of the One who "spread out the earth upon the waters," an image of a controlled and stable creation. Job 37:18 asks if one can "spread out the heavens, as solid as a molten mirror," a wonder of solidity.
4. The word can designate coating or soldering: in Isaiah 40:19, one "solders silver chains" to an idol covered with gold — an image of the futility of human work in the face of God.
5. In contexts of protest or denial, one "claps hands" — a gesture of spreading and emotional amplification that accompanies indignation or contempt (Ezekiel 6:11, 25:6).
H7554.origine: The Hebrew verb רָקַע comes from a root that evokes the action of striking or hitting. The primary image is that of hammering: one strikes, spreads, flattens. The word is related to other verbs of vigorous and decisive action. It is a concrete verb, rooted in the gestures of metalworking and daily labor.
H7554.emploi: The verb appears 11 times in the Hebrew Bible, especially in legal texts (Exodus), historical narratives (2 Samuel), and prophetic poetry (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Psalms, Job). In the context of the tabernacle and the temple (Exodus, Numbers), it describes the making of ornaments in precious metals — an activity of value and precision. In wisdom and prophetic poetry, it becomes a cosmic image: God "spreads out" the heavens and the earth at the moment of creation, an act of immense power (Psalms 136:6, Isaiah 42:5, 44:24). In contexts of judgment or conflict, it expresses the crushing of enemies or nations (2 Samuel 22:43, Ezekiel). The meaning evolves from the concrete (the goldsmith's craft) to the figurative (divine creation and dominion).
H7554.portee: This word reminds us that creation is an act of unfolding and mastery, not a chance occurrence: God "spreads out" the universe with the firmness of a divine craftsman. It also invites reflection on human work, whether it be the beautiful crafting of sacred ornaments or the exercise of divine justice against enemies. Finally, the image of flattened metal evokes transformation through suffering or discipline — an implicit theme in biblical poetry.

sens: Flat surface obtained by beating or hammering a metal
Coating or covering of surfaces
H7555.detail:
1. The word describes the action of beating or stretching a metal to form a flat and thin surface — as one forges a sheet of gold or silver by striking it with a hammer. In Numbers 16:38, the censers of the rebels Korah, Dathan, and Abiram are hammered to form flattened sheets that cover the altar of the Lord: this worked metal becomes a sacred object and a testimony.
2. The word also designates the result of this work: the flat and thin surface obtained by hammering, which serves to cover or adorn. The "extent" of the censers, transformed into metal plates, illustrates how God sanctifies even the instruments of sin by converting them into a testimony of His power and authority.
H7555.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means "to beat," "to strike," or "to spread out" — the image is that of the blacksmith who strikes the metal to flatten it. This hammering work produced the sheets and plates used in the worship of the tabernacle: the angels of the golden mercy seat, the utensils of the altar, and the bronze coverings of the altars. The same root appears in other contexts describing the stretching or spreading of surfaces.
H7555.emploi: The word appears only once in the Old Testament, in Numbers 16:38. It specifically designates the forged metal plates made from the censers of the rebels who challenged Moses and contested Aaron's priesthood. These censers, instead of being destroyed or abandoned, are transformed by hammering into sheets that cover the altar of the Lord, a symbol of consecration and sanctification. This unique context reveals that the word is used to express a transformation of profane or sin-related objects into sacred elements of worship.
H7555.portee: This word reminds us that nothing is lost with God: even the instruments of sin and rebellion can be transformed and sanctified to serve His worship. The metal platform formed by the censers of the rebels becomes a memorial engraved in the tabernacle, reminding Israel of the seriousness of contesting the authority that God has established. This transformation illustrates how God converts judgment into a teaching lesson and an invitation to faithfulness.

sens: to expel saliva from the mouth
to show contempt or disgust through this gesture
H7556.detail:
1. To spit means to expel saliva from the mouth. The text in Leviticus 15:8 literally refers to a physical act: someone "spits" on another person.
2. In the Bible, spitting on someone is a sign of deep contempt or disgust. It is a gesture that humiliates and defiles. Leviticus 15:8 shows this: the person on whom one has spat becomes ritually unclean until evening, illustrating the moral and physical impurity associated with this act of disdain.
H7556.origine: The Hebrew word rāqaq comes from a root that imitates the sound and action of spitting. It is a concrete, descriptive word that directly relates to the bodily gesture. It has few cognates in Hebrew, but it conveys a direct and universal physical reality.
H7556.emploi: The word appears only once in the preserved Hebrew Bible, in Leviticus 15:8, at the heart of a law of ritual impurity. There, it describes an act of saliva projection that renders the recipient unclean. The context shows that spitting is not a mere reflex, but a deliberate gesture carrying ritual defilement and degrading intent.
H7556.portee: Spitting in the Bible symbolizes contempt and extreme humiliation. Understanding this gesture helps grasp the horror of Christ's sufferings: during his passion, he endured spitting, which represented not only physical pain but the pinnacle of dishonor and degradation. It is a reminder of the depth of the humiliation he accepted.

sens: Fortified city of the tribe of Naphtali
H7557.detail: Rakkath is a fortified city that belonged to the territory of the tribe of Naphtali in the Promised Land. It is mentioned in the list of cities assigned to Naphtali during the division of the land (Joshua 19:35). This city is also known by another name: Tiberias, the famous city later built on the shores of the Sea of Galilee, which would become an important center of Jewish life and the New Testament.
H7557.origine: The name Rakkath means "shore" in Hebrew, which corresponds to its geographical location near the shores of the Sea of Galilee. The city was later renamed Tiberias (Τιβεριάς in Greek) when Herod Antipas rebuilt it in the early first century.
H7557.emploi: Rakkath is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Joshua 19:35, in the context of enumerating the fortified cities assigned to the tribe of Naphtali. It appears alongside other cities in the same territory such as Ziddim, Tser, and Hammath. After this biblical mention, the city became known in later history as Tiberias.

sens: Official permission granted by an authority
Right or consent given to act or undertake something
H7558.detail:
1. This word denotes official permission, that is, the agreement given by someone who has the authority to do so. In Ezra 3:7, it refers to the authorization of King Cyrus allowing the Jews to bring cedar wood from Lebanon for the reconstruction of the Temple — without this official permission, the project could not have progressed.
2. More broadly, it is the right or consent given to someone to do something. Authorization implies that without it, the action would be prohibited or illegitimate; with it, it becomes possible and legitimate.
H7558.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes the idea of "letting free" or "allowing." It is an administrative or official term that appears rarely in the Bible — only once — and refers to situations where a higher authority (King Cyrus in this case) gives its consent for an important action to be undertaken.
H7558.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Ezra 3:7. The context is historical: after the exile to Babylon, the Persian king Cyrus authorizes the Jews to return and rebuild the Temple in Jerusalem. The authorization mentioned in the text specifically concerns the importation of cedar wood from Lebanon, a crucial raw material for the construction work. This passage shows how a significant religious and political project entirely depends on the consent and will of the one who holds power.
H7558.portee: This word reminds us that every significant human endeavor requires authorizations and permissions — whether civil, political, or spiritual. For the reader, it is a lesson on respecting established order and the necessity of consent from competent authorities. In the story of Ezra, the king's authorization also shows how God can work through the decisions of the powerful to fulfill His plans.

sens: To mark something in writing on a surface
To record, officially note
H7559.detail:
1. To inscribe means to trace letters or signs on a material (paper, parchment, stone) so that the text remains and is readable. It is the action of writing itself. In Daniel 10:21, the angel speaks of what is "written in the book of truth": this book contains information inscribed, fixed in writing for future consultation.
2. Figuratively, to inscribe means to officially record, to permanently consign something in a register or document. This implies that what is written cannot be easily forgotten or erased; it is a lasting trace of a decision or event.
H7559.origine: The Hebrew verb rashah comes from a root evoking the action of marking, engraving, or tracing. The corresponding Aramaic form (resham) has the same meaning. These words are related to the world of administration and official documentation: to write was to fix the will of kings or authorities in a way that it persists and imposes itself.
H7559.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Hebrew text of Daniel, in Daniel 10:21. The angel Michael comforts the prophet Daniel by telling him that everything concerning the destinies of kingdoms and peoples is already inscribed in the "book of truth." This context reveals that "to inscribe" here means to fix in writing realities that do not change, which are established in advance in a celestial and immutable register. The word emphasizes the permanence and authority of what is written.
H7559.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us that the history of the world and the destinies of nations are not random, but are consigned in a divine plan established in advance and inscribed in God's register. It invites trust in God's sovereignty, even in the face of political upheavals or opposing powers: what is to happen has already been written in heaven.

sens: Mark signs on a surface, notably to write or inscribe words
Draft an official act, an edict that binds those who receive it
H7560.detail:
1. Trace means to make marks on a surface — to write, draw, inscribe. It is the physical action of the hand that engraves or writes. In Daniel 5:24, mysterious fingers trace writing on the wall of King Belshazzar's palace; in verse 25, we see the writing that has been traced: the words 'Numbered, numbered, weighed, and divided.'
2. To trace a decree means to draft and sign an official act that becomes law — something written, authorized, irrevocable. In Daniel 6:8-9, King Darius writes a decree that forbids praying to any god or man except the king for thirty days; it is a written and signed order that applies to all. The decree traced once cannot be changed, according to the law of the Medes and Persians.
H7560.origine: The Aramaic verb resham comes from a root that evokes the action of marking, engraving, leaving a visible trace. It is used exclusively here in the Aramaic of the New Testament (actually in the Aramaic of Daniel) to designate the action of inscribing or writing a text, an order, something that imposes itself in writing.
H7560.emploi: This verb appears only in the book of Daniel (7 occurrences), particularly during the famous scene of the mysterious writing on the wall (Daniel 5) and during the drafting of the royal decree against prayer (Daniel 6). In Daniel 5, it refers to the supernatural writing that the finger of God traces on the wall. In Daniel 6, it concerns royal decrees that the king writes and that become immutable laws. The word always applies to something written, official, that imposes itself once traced.
H7560.portee: This word reminds the reader of the power of the written word — what is traced, written, signed becomes fixed and binds the one who wrote it. For the believer, it is an image of the weight of words and actions: once written, they persist. It is also in Daniel a sign that God is above human powers — His writing, traced supernaturally, overturns kingdoms; while human decrees, although traced, can do nothing against those who obey the true God.

sens: To be wicked, to act maliciously
To be guilty, to deserve condemnation
To declare someone guilty, to condemn them in court
To act against justice or the will of God
H7561.detail:
1. The primary meaning is that of active wickedness: to act badly, to commit iniquity. It is the behavior of one who willfully transgresses the laws of God or men. In 1 Kings 8:47, the captive people confess: 'We have committed iniquities, we have done evil,' acknowledging their past malice.

2. To be guilty means to be in a state of guilt before God or justice: to have violated the established order and deserve condemnation. Job 9:20 expresses this idea: 'If I am innocent, He will declare me guilty,' showing that guilt is a judgment pronounced against someone.

3. To condemn someone in court means to officially declare them guilty, to recognize them as responsible for a fault and to impute the consequences to them. In Exodus 22:9, the one whom God 'will condemn' must repay double, applying a legal sentence.

4. On a moral and religious level, to condemn means to judge as contrary to justice and the will of God, whether one is a human judge or God Himself. In Proverbs 12:2, 'The Lord condemns the one who is full of wickedness': it is a divine act of judgment.
H7561.origine: The verb comes from a Hebrew root that carries the idea of guilt and transgression. The family of words includes the noun שָׁעַע (rasha), meaning 'wicked' or 'ungodly.' This root expresses the overturning of the just order: one who acts thus makes themselves guilty and exposes themselves to judgment. The Hebrew verb focuses less on an abstract legal process than on the moral and religious reality of being at fault before God.
H7561.emploi: This verb appears 34 times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily in the wisdom books (Job, Proverbs, Psalms) and in historical narratives. It first designates the simple fact of acting badly or being wicked; then, in a judicial context, the act of declaring someone guilty (Exodus 22:9, Deuteronomy 25:1, 1 Kings 8:32). Job frequently uses it to express the anguish of being unjustly condemned despite his innocence (Job 9:20, 10:2, 10:7). The Psalms use it to affirm that God does not condemn the righteous (Psalms 37:33). The word thus oscillates between the malicious action itself and the resulting judgment.
H7561.portee: This word reminds us that sin is never a private matter: it makes us guilty before God and before the community. It invites the believer to take divine judgment seriously, not out of servile fear, but out of reverence for the just order that God establishes. It also emphasizes that God judges with certainty: no one can contradict His verdict, unlike human judgments, which are often unjust. Finally, it shows that honest confession of sin (as in 1 Kings 8:47) is the way to restoration with God.

sens: Criminal, violent, unjust act or behavior against others
Character of one who commits evil, moral guilt
Moral evil in general, opposition to divine justice
Habitual practice of crime and injustice
System or way of life based on evil
H7562.detail:
1. Wickedness primarily refers to a criminal and violent act or series of acts: it is the harm done to one's neighbor by force or deceit. In 1 Samuel 24:14, David refuses to kill Saul, saying 'wickedness comes from the wicked,' distinguishing the evil act from the one who commits it.
2. The word also describes the guilty character of the wicked, their moral guilt: one who acts badly accumulates wickedness within them. Isaiah 58:6 speaks of 'loosing the chains of wickedness,' as if it binds the oppressors.
3. Wickedness directly opposes justice: Ecclesiastes 3:16 observes that 'in the place established for justice there is wickedness,' showing that they are incompatible.
4. It is a habit, a practice of evil: Proverbs 4:17 says 'the path of the wicked,' suggesting a road they regularly follow.
5. Sometimes it is a systematic way of life: Psalms 84:11 contrasts 'the tents of wickedness' with the temple of God, as two dwellings, two opposing worlds.
H7562.origine: The Hebrew word réshaʿ comes from a root that fundamentally means 'to be guilty' or 'to be condemnable.' It is related to the idea of legal and moral guilt: one who commits evil exposes themselves to condemnation. Wickedness is therefore not just simple malice, but concrete guilt: it makes a person liable for justice. The same word can also designate the wicked one themselves, the guilty person.
H7562.emploi: The word appears 29 times in the Old Testament, especially in the wisdom books (Proverbs, Job, Ecclesiastes) and the Psalms. It designates either the act of evil (Deuteronomy 9:27, where Moses pleads with God not to look at the wickedness of the people), or the character of the wicked (Job 34:8, 'he associates with the wicked'), or the system or order based on evil (Psalms 84:11, 'the tents of wickedness'). In Proverbs, it constantly opposes wisdom and justice: the wise flee from it, the wicked cultivate it (Proverbs 8:7). Among the prophets, it is often social injustice and the oppression of the weak that is called wickedness (Isaiah 58:6, Jeremiah 14:20).
H7562.portee: Wickedness is presented not as a fatality, but as guilt: one who commits it engages themselves toward divine judgment. For the Christian reader, this word reminds us that evil is never neutral or invisible to God: He takes it into account and will judge it. But it is also a call: God calls His servants to detach themselves from wickedness and to work towards its disappearance, notably by freeing the oppressed (Isaiah 58:6).

sens: a person guilty of a crime or fault
a person hostile to God and His law
a person who acts against justice and good
H7563.detail:
1. The wicked is primarily one who has committed a crime or fault, one who is objectively guilty. Exodus 2:13 shows a man striking his companion: he is a wicked man, a criminal. This is why Deuteronomy 25:1 and 1 Kings 8:32 speak of justifying the righteous and condemning the wicked before the tribunal.
2. But the word also designates one who refuses the law of God and opposes Him. Psalms 50:16 describes a wicked person who enumerates the laws of the Lord with his mouth but ignores them in his life: he knows the commandments but despises them. This is a deliberate hostility towards God.
3. The wicked is one whose actions harm others and destroy justice. Proverbs 15:9 states that "the way of the wicked is an abomination to the Lord": this is not just a flaw, it is a life choice contrary to what is right. Isaiah 5:23 denounces those who "justify the guilty for a bribe," meaning those who pervert justice itself.
H7563.origine: The Hebrew word רָשַׁע (rascha) likely comes from a root meaning "to violate" or "to transgress." It is related to the idea of crossing a boundary, rejecting the established order. The wicked is one who exceeds limits and acts against the laws of God and the community. In biblical Hebrew, the wicked stands in opposition to the righteous (צַדִּיק, tsaddiq): this is a fundamental contrast in the wisdom of Israel.
H7563.emploi: This word appears 249 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in Psalms, Proverbs, and the book of Job. The Psalms constantly use it to describe those whom God judges and can destroy: "the way of the wicked will perish" (Psalms 1:6). The book of Job uses it to explore the problem of evil and justice: why do the wicked prosper? (Job 21:7). Proverbs systematically contrasts it with the righteous in moral maxims: "the curse of the Lord is in the house of the wicked" (Proverbs 3:33). Genesis 18:23-25 shows Abraham pleading with God: "Will you destroy the righteous with the wicked?"—already forming the central contrast.
H7563.portee: This word invites the reader to discern between the righteous and the wicked, not as a fixed category but as a direction of life: do we walk according to God's commandments or reject them? It also reminds us that God sees hidden guilt and dishonesty, and He will hold us accountable. For the Christian, it is a call not to sit "in the company of mockers" (Psalms 1:1), but to pursue righteousness, knowing that God judges.

sens: The state of one who acts against justice and righteousness
Guilt attached to a wicked act
Malice, intention or corrupt nature
Ruin and destruction brought by evil
H7564.detail:
1. Wickedness is primarily acting contrary to the right and order desired by God. In Deuteronomy 9:4, God drives out the nations before Israel "because of the wickedness of these nations," not because Israel deserves it. It is a perverse conduct in relationships with others and with God.
2. It is also the objective guilt attached to that act. In Deuteronomy 25:2, the judge strikes the guilty party "with a number of blows proportional to the severity of his fault"—the word measures the weight, the reality of the evil committed.
3. Wickedness is a disposition of the heart, a corrupt nature that leads to evil. In Ezekiel 18:27, the wicked can "turn from his wickedness and practice righteousness and justice," which shows that it is an internal orientation, a habit of evil that one can leave behind.
4. It inevitably produces ruin. In Proverbs 13:6, "wickedness brings ruin to the sinner"—evil sows its own destruction, while "righteousness preserves the one whose way is upright."
H7564.origine: The Hebrew word רִשְׁעָה (rish.ah) comes from the root רשע (rasha) which means "to be wicked, to act badly." This root evokes the idea of turning away, deviating from the right path. In the Hebrew Bible, it appears in various forms: רָשָׁע (rashah, the adjective "wicked"), רֶשַׁע (reshe, the abstract noun "wickedness"), and our term רִשְׁעָה which emphasizes the state or act of wickedness. The word never designates a mere weakness, but always a moral revolt against the will of God.
H7564.emploi: This word appears 15 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the prophetic books (Ezekiel, Zechariah, Malachi) and in Wisdom (Proverbs). In Deuteronomy, it justifies God's judgments against the Canaanite nations. In Ezekiel 18, it is at the heart of the theology of personal responsibility: each person dies for his own wickedness, but each can also turn from it and live. In Proverbs, it systematically opposes righteousness and uprightness, not as a mere error but as a power of destruction. The term can refer to both the wickedness of a nation and that of an individual, as well as the act and the internal state from which it proceeds.
H7564.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us that evil is not an abstraction or an excusable weakness, but a reality that destroys. It also teaches that one cannot hide behind past wickedness: in Ezekiel 18, God promises life to the one who turns from evil and embraces righteousness. It is a word of responsibility, but also of hope—one is never trapped in their guilt.

sens: Intense heat, flame or spark springing from fire
A trait or arrow shot with violence
Fever, illness or affliction that strikes someone
Passionate impulse, emotional intensity
H7565.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes the intense heat of fire, the spark that leaps: Job 5:7 compares man born to suffering to the spark that "flies," an image of a reality that rises quickly and inevitably.
2. By extension, it names the traits or arrows of war: Psalms 76:4 enumerates the weapons of battle ("arrows," shield, sword), fervor becoming a destructive projectile launched in combat.
3. The word can also refer to an affliction that strikes—fever or plague—as a sudden and devastating blow: Deuteronomy 32:24 groups "fever" among the punishments (hunger, violent diseases), and Habakkuk 3:5 sees "plague" marching before God.
4. On an emotional and spiritual level, fervor becomes intense passion: Song of Solomon 8:6 describes the "fervors" of love as an unquenchable fire, a force as absolute as death and the grave.
H7565.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root expressing brightness and heat. Its primary image is that of a flame that rises and leaps—the spark that flies or burns. The same root is found in Reseph, a Canaanite god associated with plague and lightning in the ancient Levantine pantheons, which shows that the notion of destructive fervor was central to the concept. The word appears mainly in biblical poetry and wisdom texts.
H7565.emploi: The word appears six times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily in poetry (Psalms, Song, Habakkuk) and in solemn discourse (Deuteronomy 32). It takes on various faces depending on the context: fervor can be physical and destructive (fever, pestilence, war arrow), or passionate and spiritual (the intensity of divine love). Deuteronomy 32:24 and Habakkuk 3:5 place it among punishments and signs of divine power; Song of Solomon 8:6 exalts it as an expression of the strength of love. Job 5:7 uses it as a proverbial image of inevitable human suffering.
H7565.portee: This word reminds us that God possesses a power that manifests as fervor—whether it be the fire of judgment or the consuming fire of love. For the reader, it invites recognition of the absolute intensity of the divine reality: one cannot remain indifferent before God. It also teaches that authentic love, like that described in the Song, burns with an irreducible force, as absolute as death itself.

sens: Son of Ephraim, from the tribe of Ephraim during the divided monarchy
H7566.detail: Resheph is a man from the tribe of Ephraim mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 7:25. He appears in a genealogy where he is presented as the son of Rephach and the father of Telach, being part of the lineage of Ephraim, one of the sons of Joseph.
H7566.origine: The name Resheph means "flame" in Hebrew. It shares the same root as words denoting fire or spark, thus evoking liveliness and fervor. This name, borne by several individuals in the Old Testament, belonged to families of the people of Israel.
H7566.emploi: Resheph is mentioned only once in the entire Bible, in 1 Chronicles 7:25, in a genealogical list of the tribe of Ephraim covering the period of the divided monarchy. He is simply cited as a link in a family chain: son of Rephach and father of Telach. No action or event is attributed to him; it is merely a genealogical mention.

sens: To strike, to beat violently something to annihilate it
To reduce to nothing, to completely ruin
To be brought down, to be reduced to nothing
H7567.detail:
1. The word first describes the action of striking or mistreating something or someone in a destructive manner, like when one strikes grain to separate it from the chaff — here, it is striking to destroy. In Jeremiah 5:17, the enemy "will destroy" the strong cities: he crushes them, pulverizes them through military violence.
2. It is also the state of complete ruin, annihilation: something prosperous becomes nothing, disappears. In Malachi 1:4, the Edomites say: "We are destroyed" — they acknowledge that their land is in ruins, crushed by divine judgment.
3. The word can express the passive condition, being reduced to nothing, being crushed. This is what those who resist God suffer: the Lord restores the ruins, but to overturn them again, for the land remains cursed.
H7567.origine: The Hebrew word רָשַׁשׁ (rashash) comes from a root that means to strike or to grind. It is found in the language of the ancient Near East to describe the action of devastating a territory or reducing a city to dust. Its image is that of a hammer or ram striking the walls: it breaks, it annihilates, nothing remains. It is a word of destructive violence, often applied to God's judgment or the ravages of war.
H7567.emploi: This Hebrew verb appears only twice in the French Bible, both translated as "destroy." In Jeremiah 5:17, it describes how a conquering enemy ravages a land: it destroys the harvests, the babies, the animals, and especially the walled cities — an image of total desolation. In Malachi 1:4, it evokes the ruined state of Edom, a people enemy of the Lord: even if its inhabitants rebuild, the Lord will destroy again. Both uses depict divine judgment: God uses destruction as an instrument of punishment, or promises that attempts to rebuild what He has destroyed will fail.
H7567.portee: This word reminds the reader that there is a real, concrete judgment: God is not absent or indifferent to evil. His warnings are not empty. But it also speaks of a serious threat: when the Lord "destroys," it is because of persistent sin, as with the Edomites. For the believer, it is an invitation to fear God, to listen to Him, and not to assume that their ruins will be restored without repentance.

sens: Fishing or hunting net, to catch animals or fish
Bronze lattice or trellis for the altar of the tabernacle
Trap or hidden danger that ensnares one who gets caught in it
Judgment of God that envelops and captures the guilty
Temptations or malevolent influences that lead to sin
H7568.detail:
1. The net is primarily a concrete object: a fishing or hunting net woven to capture living animals. Proverbs 1:17 speaks of casting a net before the eyes of birds to catch them.
2. In the tabernacle, the word refers to the woven bronze lattice or trellis, an architectural structure of the altar for burnt offerings (Exodus 27:4).
3. The net becomes an image of the trap or hidden danger: one who walks on it gets ensnared and cannot escape (Job 18:8: "he puts his feet on a net, he walks in the meshes").
4. The net symbolizes God's judgment that envelops the wicked on all sides (Psalms 35:8: "let them be caught in the net they have laid").
5. The net also represents the temptations or corrupting influences of wicked leaders that lead the people into sin (Hosea 5:1 speaks of a net laid for the leaders and the people).
H7568.origine: The Hebrew word רֶשֶׁת (reshet) comes from a root that evokes the idea of weaving or braiding. In the Hebrew language, this word belongs to the family of words that describe interwoven or intertwined structures. The net is the perfect image: an object made of interwoven meshes, inevitable once one is caught in it. This word appears 21 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the Psalms and Proverbs, where it becomes a powerful image of judgment and sin.
H7568.emploi: The word appears 21 times, primarily in the Psalms (8 times), Proverbs (2 times), and the prophets Ezekiel, Hosea, Jeremiah. It has two distinct uses: first, a concrete and architectural sense (Exodus 27:4-5 and 38:4 for the lattice of the altar), then very quickly a dominant figurative sense. In the Psalms and Proverbs, the net becomes an image of the trap of sin and divine judgment: it is "laid" (Psalms 35:8), one "walks in it" (Job 18:8), one prays to the Lord to deliver us from it (Psalms 25:15). In the prophets (Ezekiel, Hosea), God Himself "spreads" His net over the nations or guilty kings to capture them (Ezekiel 12:13, 17:20). The net is often what one has laid oneself (Psalms 35:8) and which turns against oneself.
H7568.portee: This word teaches the believer a profound truth: the sin and malice one sows become a trap for oneself. One who lays nets to ensnare others finds themselves caught (Psalms 35:8). Conversely, the psalmist learns to implore the Lord to be delivered from them (Psalms 25:15, 31:5), discovering that only God can rescue us from the hidden traps of evil. It is a call to vigilance and trust: not to fear the secret nets of enemies, but to seek the protection of the Lord.

sens: Link composed of interlocking rings or meshes
Shackle, instrument of captivity or punishment
H7569.detail: 1. The chain is primarily a material object: a series of linked rings or meshes. In Solomon's temple, gold chains adorn the sanctuary to suspend a veil (1 Kings 6:21), showing both the practical and precious aspect of this object. 2. The chain takes on a figurative meaning when it symbolizes captivity and constraint. The prophet Ezekiel, speaking of God's judgment on Jerusalem, calls to "prepare the chains," for the entire land will be delivered to violence and chaos, carried away by misfortune like a prisoner in his fetters (Ezekiel 7:23).
H7569.origine: The Hebrew word rattoq comes from a root that evokes braiding or intertwining. The starting image is that of the meshes of a chain knotted together. The word appears in a closely related feminine form, rattiqah (רַתִּיקָה), with the same meaning. Both forms refer to the same object: a chain, whether used to adorn the temple or to bind prisoners.
H7569.emploi: The word rattoq appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible. The first time in a context of luxury and beauty (1 Kings 6:21), where the chains are made of gold and decorative; the second time in a context of judgment and misfortune (Ezekiel 7:23), where they become a symbol of servitude and divine punishment. This variation in usage shows that the same object can be wealth or calamity, depending on the context and God's judgment.
H7569.portee: The chain reminds us of two opposing spiritual truths: on one hand, that God can adorn and sanctify His temple with beauty; on the other hand, that sin and violence inevitably attract divine judgment, which chains the people to its consequences. This word invites the reader to meditate on the difference between the freedom given by obedience to God and the slavery brought by sin.

sens: To be boiling, to enter into tumultuous agitation
To boil, to bring to a boil
To express an intense emotion that stirs within
H7570.detail:
1. The primary meaning is that of a liquid that boils: water or another liquid becomes agitated due to heat, producing bubbles and tumultuous movement. In Ezekiel 24:5, we see a pot that must "boil with vigorous boiling" so that the meat and bones can cook. It is the image of visible and noisy boiling.
2. The verb can also mean "to cause to boil" or "to bring to a boil": it is to act so that something enters into a bubbling movement. In Job 41:22, the leviathan (the great crocodile or sea monster) "boils the depths of the sea like a pot"—it causes extreme agitation of the ocean by its fearsome strength.
3. Figuratively, the word expresses an emotion that rises, bubbling internally: in Job 30:27, the suffering person says that their "bowels boil incessantly"—it is the internal agitation of pain, grief, or indignation that rises from deep within and does not subside.
H7570.origine: The Hebrew verb רָתַח (ratach) belongs to the family of words that describe agitation and tumult. It evokes the sensory image of boiling: noise, movement, heat. It is an onomatopoeic or imitative word in a sense, which reproduces through its sound the idea of boiling. In the Old Testament, this verb is infrequent and remains attached to this image of physical or emotional boiling.
H7570.emploi: The verb appears three times in the Old Testament, all in different contexts that show the richness of its use. In Ezekiel 24:5, it literally describes the cooking of meats in a pot, in an oracle that makes this meal a symbol of the judgment of Jerusalem. In Job 41:22, it depicts the overwhelming power of the leviathan capable of boiling the waters like a cauldron. In Job 30:27, it shifts to the emotional sense: the bowels of the suffering righteous boil with continual pain. The word thus alternates between a concrete sense (cooking), an image of indomitable natural force (the monster of the depths), and an expression of the inner agitation of the soul.
H7570.portee: This word helps us see that the Bible does not shy away from intense emotions: pain, anger, or indignation boil within us without it being a sin. Job bluntly expresses that his bowels boil—he laments, he suffers, and that is true and permitted. At the same time, the image of boiling reminds us that the forces of evil and chaos are turbulent and restless (like the leviathan), while calm and peace belong to those who put their trust in God.

sens: To bring a liquid to a boil due to heat
To cook vigorously in a container
Tumultuous boiling of a cooking liquid
H7571.detail:
1. The word describes the physical and visible action: a liquid that boils, producing bubbles under intense heat. In Ezekiel 24:5, it is commanded to boil the meat vigorously in a pot, evoking the image of an intense fire beneath the container.
2. It is also the result: a tumultuous broth, a vigorous cooking where meat and bones cook together. The word emphasizes the massive, even violent, nature of this cooking.
3. The boiling itself, this visible agitation of water rising in steam, can figuratively evoke a situation of turmoil or effervescence, although this sense is not developed here.
H7571.origine: The Hebrew root paints the image of a turbulent and rising movement: the boiling that bursts forth. It is related to other Hebrew words describing agitated or tumultuous movements. The context of domestic cooking and the vocabulary of the pot ("pot", "fire") show that it was a familiar image to the people of Israel, common in ancient cooking.
H7571.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Ezekiel 24:5, in a passage of great symbolic weight. The prophet Ezekiel is commanded to mime the siege of Jerusalem by putting meat in a pot and boiling it vigorously. This image concretely translates, through a prophetic theatrical act, the horror and violence of divine judgment on the city. The violent boiling thus becomes a metaphor for turmoil and destruction.
H7571.portee: This image of violent boiling serves to make tangible and unforgettable the judgment of God. It reminds us that the prophetic word is not vague or abstract: it is anchored in sensory experience, in what everyone knows (a boiling pot). This moves the prophet's message from the theoretical realm to that of lived horror, inviting the people to take the divine warning seriously.

sens: To attach an animal to a vehicle or object to pull it
To actively prepare something for use or action
H7573.detail:
1. To harness means to fix a domestic animal (horse, donkey, ox) to a cart, plow, or harness, using straps or harnesses, so that it can pull it. In Micah 1:13, the prophet addresses the king of Israel with a sharp word: "Harness the steeds to your chariot," meaning prepare to flee at a gallop, for judgment is coming.
2. By extension, the verb evokes the idea of preparing something with eagerness or urgency, getting ready to act. The image of suddenly harnessing horses suggests a rapid and determined mobilization, like that of a warrior preparing for battle or a king fleeing from the enemy.
H7573.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the action of binding, assembling, or fixing together. The verb concretely describes the act of fastening the straps and traces that connect the animal to the cart. This root is rare in the Hebrew Bible: it appears only once, in this passage from Micah where it paints the dramatic urgency of royal flight.
H7573.emploi: The verb is used only once throughout the Bible, in Micah 1:13. The prophet employs it in a woe oracle against the cities of the northern kingdom. The context is that of an imminent invasion: the kings and military leaders must flee hastily, and the prophet ironically calls them to harness their war horses. It is a verb from the concrete and martial vocabulary, rooted in the daily life of the time.
H7573.portee: This word reminds us that the Bible often speaks the language of familiar images: a harnessed chariot, a hurried flight. It does not hide the consequences of sin and the judgment of God. For the reader, it also illustrates the urgency with which God calls His people to turn from Him or to suffer the visible and immediate consequences.

sens: Low shrub of the desert, with white and hard wood
Wood used as fuel or to make hot charcoal
By extension, a symbol of poverty or distress
H7574.detail:
1. The broom is a small shrub found in arid and desert regions of the Middle East. It has dense, white wood, few leaves, and grows low to the ground. Elijah sat under a broom in the desert after fleeing from Jezebel (1 Kings 19:4), just as one seeks shelter under any shrub in arid lands.
2. The wood of the broom burns well and produces very hot charcoal: Psalm 120:4 mentions the "burning coals of the broom" to evoke the destructive heat of wicked words. Thus, it is valued as fuel and for making intense fire.
3. In Job 30:4, the poor uproot the roots of the broom to eat them, which shows that this plant represents extreme poverty and hunger: one only eats the roots of a broom when there is nothing else.
H7574.origine: The Hebrew word rethem literally refers to this characteristic shrub of the deserts of the Levant. It is a well-known plant among the inhabitants of the region, mentioned several times in the Bible for its two qualities: its ability to provide scant shade in the desert and its excellent burning wood. The word remains stable across all biblical texts.
H7574.emploi: The word appears four times in the Bible, only in contexts of crisis or solitude. Elijah uses it as a temporary shelter in the desert when he flees danger (1 Kings 19:4-5): it is the only natural refuge nearby. In Psalm 120:4, the broom symbolizes destructive violence, its embers representing human malice. In Job 30:4, it is the plant of the hungry, those who have no other food. Each time, the broom appears as a minimalist resource, linked to adversity.
H7574.portee: The broom reminds us that even in the desert, God provides what we need: Elijah finds shade and rest under this humble shrub. This modest plant also speaks to the fragility of human life and the resources we share with the poor. It invites the reader to recognize that God cares for us, even when we are at the end of our strength.

sens: Camping site of the people of Israel in the desert during the Exodus
H7575.detail: 1. Rithma is a stopping place mentioned twice in the account of Israel's journey through the desert after leaving Egypt. It is a stage in the long journey that lasted forty years. It appears in the list of successive encampments of the people, between Hazeroth and Rimmon-Perez (Numbers 33:18-19).
H7575.origine: The name Rithma means "broom" or "heath," a desert plant. It is likely a place known for the bush vegetation found there. Its exact location is uncertain, but it would be situated northeast of Hazeroth, in the Sinai region.
H7575.emploi: Rithma appears only twice in the Bible, both in chapter 33 of the book of Numbers, which enumerates all forty-two stages of Israel's journey in the desert. These two mentions (verses 18 and 19) simply show that Israel camped there before moving on to the next encampment. No particular event occurs at this location: it is just a stop along the way.

sens: To break or sever a bond that holds something together
To be chained, carried as a prisoner
H7576.detail:
