1. The word expresses the action of detaching or breaking what holds things together. In Ecclesiastes, the "silver cord" that "is detached" evokes the fragility of human life: the cord symbolizes one of the last links that holds the soul to the body, and its rupture represents the inevitable death. It is a poetic image of the end of all earthly existence.
2. The word can also mean to be chained or burdened with chains, particularly in a context of captivity or constraint. In Nahum, the nobles of a city are "burdened" with chains: they become prisoners, bound by the enemy's force. This is the opposite image of the first meaning — here, one is not freed, but rather bound and subjected.
H7576.origine: The Hebrew root evokes the idea of tying, binding, or breaking a link. It belongs to a group of Hebrew verbs expressing actions of rupture or detachment. The context and grammatical construction of the verb (active or passive) determine whether the emphasis is on the action of detaching or on the state of being bound. This alternation of meaning — from detachment to binding — reflects the natural ambiguity of linking verbs in Hebrew.
H7576.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible, in very different contexts. In Ecclesiastes 12:8, it describes the rupture of the silver cord, one of the images of meditation on death and return to dust. In Nahum 3:10, it refers to the humiliation of the nobles of Nineveh, chained during the city's fall. These two uses show how the same Hebrew verb can shift from one meaning to another depending on the context: detaching on one side, chaining on the other. The absence of context in ancient grammar sometimes leaves the meaning floating between these two poles.
H7576.portee: This word invites the Christian reader to contemplate the fragility of human life and the certainty of death (Ecclesiastes). It also reminds us that all servitude has an end: even chained, the captive is not bound forever. Death breaks all earthly ties, whether those that hold us to life or those that enslave us. It is an invitation to place one's hope elsewhere than in this world.

sens: small fine metal chain
ornament or loose link
H7577.detail:
1. The word refers to a small chain, generally made of precious metal. In Isaiah 40:19, the prophet describes a craftsman who covers an idol with gold and solders silver chains to it: these small chains are luxury ornaments intended to beautify and enhance the statue.
2. Figuratively, it can evoke any fine but visible link, an element that holds or unites — but this usage remains marginal in the Bible, as the word appears only once.
H7577.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root suggesting the idea of "detaching" or "binding"; it is formed to designate the object itself: a small chain. It is a technical term in the vocabulary of metalworking and goldsmithing, particularly used in descriptions of material beauty and precious ornaments.
H7577.emploi: The word appears only once in the entire Bible, in Isaiah 40:19. The prophet uses it to describe the idea people have of the gods of the nations: wooden statues, covered with gold and adorned with silver chains. The context is satirical: Isaiah belittles the making of idols by showing it as a mere craft, where the worker rivets small precious chains to give prestige to a lifeless object. It is a concrete detail that highlights the contrast between these ephemeral ornaments and the majesty of the true God.
H7577.portee: This image of chains soldered to an idol reminds us that material beauty and prestige can mask spiritual emptiness. It invites the reader to reflect on what they place their trust in: shiny objects that are devoid of life, or the living God. It is a simple yet powerful lesson against idolatry.

sens: Intense trembling of fear
Paralyzing fear that grips
Dread in the face of a threat
Formidable presence of a power
H7578.detail: 1. The word primarily describes the physical trembling caused by extreme fear: when one is seized by terror, one trembles. In Hosea 13:1, the "terror" evokes the impressive presence of Ephraim at the height of its power: when he spoke, people trembled before him, so great was his authority. 2. It is also the intense fear, the dread that grips the soul when one feels threatened or faces a power that cannot be controlled. 3. More broadly, it encompasses anything that inspires a respectful fear and a sensation of helplessness in the face of something greater or stronger than oneself.
H7578.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that expresses the movement of trembling or vibrating. It is linked to the physical idea of shivering, the trembling of the body that accompanies fear. The initial image is very corporeal: it is what happens in the body when fear takes hold of us. The root can also evoke noise or anxious murmuring.
H7578.emploi: This word appears only once in the preserved biblical text, in Hosea 13:1. It describes the effect of the word of the kingdom of Ephraim at its peak: when he spoke, a terror, an impressive presence, emanated from him. It is a past moment that Hosea evokes as a now-lost power, contrasting with the guilt and death that followed. The rarity of the word underscores its emotional impact.
H7578.portee: This word reminds us that the true power of a people or a person does not reside in the fear they can inspire, but in obedience to God. Ephraim had this formidable presence but lost it by turning to Baal. For the reader, it is an invitation to recognize where true lasting authority lies and not to seek influence through the fear we inspire.

sens: Extract water from a well, a spring, using a container
Perform this task to provide for others
Withdraw, collect
Serve by carrying water
H7579.detail:
1. To draw is to extract water from a well or a spring, usually with a bucket or a pitcher. Rebecca "drew" water at the well (Genesis 24:20): she went down to the source, filled her container, and came back up. It is a simple, physical, concrete gesture.
2. The verb also refers to the action of seeking and bringing water for others. Rebecca "drew for all the camels" (Genesis 24:20), the men of Bethlehem "drew water from the cistern" and presented it to David (1 Chronicles 11:18).
3. To draw can also mean to collect or withdraw. Israel "drew water and poured it out before the Lord" (1 Samuel 7:6) as a sign of repentance: the act of drawing becomes symbolic.
4. In the context of servitude, drawing water is a chore: the Gibeonites become "hewers of wood and drawers of water" (Joshua 9:23), a servile function assigned to the conquered.
H7579.origine: The Hebrew verb sha'av (שָׁאַב) comes from a root that evokes the idea of pulling or extracting. It is a concrete word, rooted in the daily life of the ancient Near East, where drawing water from the source or well was a fundamental task. The word belongs to the simple language of ordinary gestures.
H7579.emploi: The verb sha'av appears 18 times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in domestic or communal contexts. It first appears in Genesis 24 (the story of Rebecca), where it describes the repeated act of drawing water. It then appears in historical accounts: in Joshua 9, it denotes servitude; in 1 Samuel 7, a ritualized act of repentance; in 1 Chronicles 11, an act of devotion. In Isaiah 12:3, the prophet invites to draw "with joy" the waters of salvation, transforming the concrete word into a spiritual image: drawing becomes receiving the blessings of God.
H7579.portee: This word roots faith in the humble gestures of daily life. Drawing water is an essential, free task, often performed by women or servants. The Bible speaks of it straightforwardly, reminding us that God values discreet service. Isaiah twists the image to invite the believer to "draw" from God's salvation with joy: spiritual life is nourished by these repeated, simple, and true gestures.

sens: To make the characteristic cry of a lion
To cry out with strength and fury, referring to a person or an army
To manifest sovereign power and authority, referring to God
To express distress, suffering, or lamentation
H7580.detail:
1. The roar of the lion is the natural and powerful cry of this animal: in Judges 14:5, the young lion comes to meet Samson "roaring," that is, letting out its terrifying cry. This roar is a sign of its brute strength.
2. The word also applies to men or peoples who let out cries of anger or violence: in Isaiah 5:29, the conqueror "roars like young lions" — he lets out furious cries as he seizes his prey, crushing everything in his path.
3. God Himself "roars" in the Bible, notably in Jeremiah 25:30, where "the Lord will roar from on high" to manifest His sovereign judgment against the earth. The roar of God is the expression of His absolute power and His fearsome voice.
4. The roar can also express pain and despair: in Psalms 38:9, the suffering person cries out, "Lord, all my desires are before you; my sighing is not hidden from you" — the inner roar of one who suffers.
H7580.origine: The Hebrew root שׁאַג (sha'ag) evokes the deep and powerful sound that resonates: the roar of the lion. The word paints the image of a strong, commanding voice that demands attention and respect through its brute force. It is akin to the idea of an energetic cry, an impressive sound emission. In the Greek translation of the Old Testament, this verb is often rendered by ὀρύομαι (oruomai), which literally means "to howl" or "to roar." The choice of this verb to also describe the action of God reveals how the Scriptures depict divine power.
H7580.emploi: The verb appears 17 times in the Scriptures. It first describes the roar of the lion (Judges 14:5, Isaiah 5:29, Jeremiah 2:15), the king of animals whose cry inspires terror. It then extends to prophets and enemies who "roar" (Ezekiel 22:25, Psalms 74:4), expressing their violence or malice. The Psalmist also uses it for his own lamentation (Psalms 38:9, Psalms 22:14): his inner cry resembles the roar of a wounded beast. But the most remarkable use is where the Lord "roars" (Jeremiah 25:30, Joel 3:16, Amos 3:8): here the roar becomes the expression of divine majesty that manifests in judgment or prophetic call.
H7580.portee: This word shows us that God's power is expressed in a language that creatures can hear and fear. The roar of the Lord is not a discreet murmur: it is a direct, audible manifestation of His sovereignty. For the believer, understanding this biblical motif of divine roaring reminds us that God is alive, active, and never silent in the face of evil or iniquity. This invites both respectful fear and assurance: the one who roars in our favor is incomparably more powerful than any threat.

sens: Powerful and deep cry of the lion
Hoarse and prolonged sound of a wild beast
Cry of human anguish or complaint
Expression of suffering or torment
Destructive noise of sin and violence
H7581.detail:
1. The roar of the lion: this impressive and sonorous call made by the lion. In Isaiah 5:29, the roar of the king of Assyria is compared to that of a lioness pouncing on her prey. This is the first meaning, the most literal.

2. Cry of a creature in action: the noise made by a beast when attacking or devastating. The roar accompanies fury and destruction — it is the sound of violence unfolding (Ezekiel 19:7: the land is destroyed "at the sound of its roars").

3. Cry of human distress: the word also applies to the cry of one who suffers. In Psalms 22:2, the psalmist asks God to listen to his complaints (the word rendered as "listen"), and in Job 3:24, his cries or sighs of pain pour out like water.

4. Groans of a broken heart: in Psalms 32:3, it is the daily groaning of one who bears the weight of guilt. The roar then becomes the inner expression of torment.

5. Cry of the wicked: in Job 4:10, the roar of lions symbolizes the brute power of the wicked, a threat that collapses.
H7581.origine: The Hebrew word שְׁאָגָה (she'agah) comes from the root שׁאג (sha'ag), which means "to roar" or "to cry." This root expresses the idea of making a hoarse and prolonged noise. The word is linked to the natural image of animal roaring, but the Bible also uses it to describe human cries of distress, showing how biblical Hebrew draws from the sounds of nature to express intense emotions.
H7581.emploi: The word appears 7 times in the Hebrew Bible, notably in the poetic books (Job, Psalms, Isaiah, Ezekiel). It first denotes the literal roar of the lion, a major creature in the biblical animal world, symbolizing power and threat (Job 4:10, Isaiah 5:29, Ezekiel 19:7). But the Bible also applies it to human suffering: the cries of the distressed psalmist, the groans of the penitent, the cry of one whom God seems to ignore. This dual usage shows that the roar becomes an image of emotional intensity, whether it be that of danger or anguish.
H7581.portee: This word reminds us that suffering is real and worthy of being heard. Just as the lion roars to manifest its strength, we spiritually roar when the weight of sin or misfortune crushes us. God hears these cries — this is the message of Psalm 22. It encourages the believer not to stifle their distress, but to cry out to God, who alone can transform it.

sens: Cause to collapse with a crash, destroy noisily
Be reduced to ruins, collapse
Leave devastated, ravaged, without inhabitants
H7582.detail:
1. The verb first evokes the noise and violence of destruction: causing strong cities to collapse, transforming them into heaps of rubble with a great crash. This is what the king of Assyria claims to accomplish when he says to Hezekiah: "you reduce strong cities to heaps of ruins" (2 Kings 19:25).
2. The word also describes the state of what has collapsed: being reduced to ruins, lying in debris. Isaiah sees the devastated cities, emptied of inhabitants, the land ravaged by solitude (Isaiah 6:11).
3. In a broader sense, it causes total desolation: transforming a fertile place into a desert, depriving it of human life. The verb captures both the moment of the blow and the permanent state that follows.
H7582.origine: The root expresses the idea of noise, crash, chaos. The Hebrew verb literally means "to make noise while collapsing." In the same family, we find the idea of violent and noisy destruction, of upheaval that leaves visible and audible traces.
H7582.emploi: The verb appears 5 times in the Old Testament, especially in Isaiah and 2 Kings, always to describe the destruction of cities or lands. It is used in the passive (to be devastated) and in the active (to reduce to ruins). In the speech of the king of Assyria (2 Kings 19:25 and Isaiah 37:26), which are parallel passages, the king boasts of having reduced strong cities to ruins. Isaiah 6:11 uses it to describe the vision of divine judgment: the cities will be devastated until they become a desert. It is always a massive and lasting destruction.
H7582.portee: This word reminds the Christian reader that the destruction of sin and rebellion is not a whisper, but a visible and definitive judgment. It also teaches humility: even strong cities, even human powers can be brought to nothing. For the believer, it is an exhortation not to trust in visible fortifications, but in the only power of God.

sens: Observe someone or something attentively
Gaze at someone intently
Examine someone to judge, evaluate
H7583.detail:
1. Observe someone or something attentively: The servant looks at Rebekah to see if she is indeed the one God has destined for Isaac. His persistent gaze seeks signs, confirmations.
2. Gaze at someone intently: This is a gaze that lasts, that persists, that scrutinizes — not just a fleeting glance. In Genesis 24:21, the man "looked" (looked continuously) in amazement.
3. Examine someone to judge, evaluate: The gaze is not neutral; it checks, it weighs the person or situation to make a decision or verify a divine promise.
H7583.origine: The Hebrew verb שָׁאָה (sha'ah) evokes the idea of directing one's attention towards something, of fixing someone intensely. Its root fundamentally expresses the physical act of looking, but in a form (the Hithpael) that emphasizes the subject's active action — one looks oneself, actively. The word belongs to the family of visual perception verbs in Hebrew.
H7583.emploi: This verb appears only once in the preserved biblical text, in Genesis 24:21. The context is that of Abraham's servant observing Rebekah after she offered him a drink and proposed to water his camels. His insistent gaze attempts to discern whether God has guided his journey to the right young woman. It is a look of expectation and verification, laden with the responsibility of finding Isaac's bride. The Hithpael emphasizes the servant's sustained attention.
H7583.portee: This word teaches us that looking is not passive: it is an active, attentive action that seeks signs of divine providence. The believer who "looks" examines the facts to recognize God's work in their life. It is a lesson in discernment: to observe with intention, weigh the clues, and wait for the confirmations that God gives to those who sincerely seek Him.

sens: the underground world where all the dead go
the grave, death itself
a place of no return
a place where God is not praised
the punishment of the wicked
extreme humiliation and degradation
H7585.detail:
1. The abode of the dead is the underground world where all the dead descend, without distinction between the righteous and the sinners: it is the afterlife as conceived in the Old Testament. Genesis 37:35 mentions Jacob who wants to "descend to his son" in the abode of the dead, understood as the common place of all the deceased.

2. The word also simply refers to the grave, death: it is the inevitable end of every living man (Ecclesiastes 9:10: "Whatever your hand finds to do, do it with all your might; for in the abode of the dead, where you are going, there is neither work nor thought nor knowledge nor wisdom").

3. It is a place of no return: Job 7:9 expresses this: "He who goes down to the abode of the dead does not come up again." This is the major characteristic: one does not return from there.

4. It is a place of silence, without praise of God: Psalms 6:6 affirms this: "In death, there is no remembrance of you; who will give you thanks in the abode of the dead?"

5. The wicked are sent there as punishment: Proverbs 5:5 speaks of the one who leads "straight to the abode of the dead" (the foreign woman), illustrating the consequence of sin.

6. Figuratively, the word describes extreme humiliation, degradation in sin: it is the image of a total and definitive fall into misery.
H7585.origine: The Hebrew word שְׁאוֹל (Sheol) primarily designates the place where one goes, the pit, the abyss: its basic image is that of an underground depth. The root evokes what is hollow or empty. Throughout the Old Testament, Sheol is the equivalent of the world of the dead, sometimes translated as "hell" in modern French, but the Segond 1910 chooses "the abode of the dead" to remain faithful to the original meaning: it is not a place of active torment, but the territory of the dead. This word appears 64 times in the Hebrew Bible, almost always to speak of the destination of every mortal.
H7585.emploi: The abode of the dead appears 64 times in the Old Testament, concentrated mainly in the Psalms, Job, and Proverbs, which meditate on death and human destiny. Jacob fears descending to the abode of the dead in mourning (Genesis 37:35, 42:38); it is also the threat attached to impious acts or divine punishment (Numbers 16:30-33: the earth opens and swallows Korah "alive to the abode of the dead"). The righteous hope to be delivered from it (Psalms 49:15: "God will redeem my soul from the power of the abode of the dead"), while sinners descend there in judgment (Proverbs 15:24: "The path of life leads to the wise, to turn him away from the abode of the dead"). Hosea 13:14 even personifies it: "I will redeem them from the power of the abode of the dead," where the word becomes almost alive, an enemy of God. It is the final destiny of every man, the great equalizer.
H7585.portee: For the Christian, the abode of the dead in the Old Testament sheds light on what Jesus has conquered through his resurrection. This ancient kingdom of silence and no return is now broken: Christ has opened the way to eternal life and resurrection. Meditating on this ancient reality shows the extent of what the Gospel changes. It also reminds us that death is serious, the stakes of sin are real, and that our hope in Christ is not an illusion, but the answer to the threat that Sheol represented.

sens: first king of Israel, from the tribe of Benjamin
son of Kish and father of Jonathan
man chosen by the prophet Samuel to reign over Israel
H7586G.detail: 1. Saul is the first king of Israel, from the tribe of Benjamin. He is presented as a remarkable young man: "young and handsome, more handsome than any of the children of Israel, and taller than any of the people" (1 Samuel 9:2). It is the Lord who designates him to save his people from the enemies that press upon them. 2. Saul is the son of Kish, a Benjamite of good family, and he becomes the father of several children, including his son Jonathan who will be his companion and a great warrior. Jonathan loves him deeply and defends him before his father (1 Samuel 20:32). 3. Saul receives the anointing from the prophet Samuel and becomes king with the mission to deliver Israel. However, he disobeys God on several occasions, notably by not fully obeying His orders regarding the complete destruction of Amalek (1 Samuel 15).
H7586G.origine: The name Saul means "asked for" or "desired" in Hebrew, from the verb שאל (sha'al) which means "to ask." It is a name that expresses the wish — the people of Israel had asked Samuel for a king, and Saul is the one that God grants them. The name thus evokes both the human desire to have a king like the other nations and God's response to that request.
H7586G.emploi: Saul appears in the Old Testament primarily in the books of 1 and 2 Samuel. He is mentioned at least 326 times. His story begins in chapter 9 of 1 Samuel when he is presented as a candidate for the throne. The narrative covers his election, his early victories against the Philistines and Amalekites, his wars, his progressive disobedience to God, and ultimately his rejection by the Lord in favor of David. Saul reigns for about forty years over Israel. After his death in the battle of Gilboa, his name remains attached to the time of Israel's emerging monarchy and contrasts with that of David, the beloved king who succeeds him.
H7586G.portee: The story of Saul teaches believers that external prestige, youth, or physical strength are not enough to serve God — obedience and humility are essential. His gradual decline shows the consequences of disobedience and refusal to listen to the prophetic word. Yet, Saul remains a king to whom God has given authority, reminding us that God governs history according to His purposes, even through the weaknesses of men.

sens: son of Simeon and a Canaanite woman
ancestor of a family of Israel
H7586H.detail:
1. Saul is a son of Simeon born in Egypt or during the Exodus, whose mother was a Canaanite. He appears in the genealogies of Israel at key moments in its history: during the descent into Egypt (Genesis 46:10), at the departure from Egypt (Exodus 6:15), and during the census in the wilderness (Numbers 26:13).
2. Through his descendants, Saul founded a family of Israel called "the Saulites" (or Shaulites), a branch of the tribe of Simeon counted among the people after the exodus from Egypt.
H7586H.origine: The name Saul means "one who is asked for" or "desired" — an image of one for whom prayers are made and awaited. It is an ordinary Hebrew name, borne by other important figures in Scripture (the first king of Israel, Saul, is the most well-known example). The form "Shaulite" (שָׁאוּלִי) simply designates the descendants of Saul, according to the Hebrew usage of family patronyms.
H7586H.emploi: Saul is mentioned four times in Scripture, each time as a name in a genealogy: in Genesis 46:10 and Exodus 6:15, among the sons of Simeon born or arrived in Egypt; in Numbers 26:13, during the census of the tribes in the wilderness; and in 1 Chronicles 4:24, in a similar enumeration. These official lists show that Saul was a recognized family leader, whose lineage continued in Israel and was counted during the censuses of the people.

sens: ancient king of Edom, successor of Samlah
man living in the time of the Patriarchs
H7586I.detail:
1. Saul was a king of Edom who reigned after Samlah. He came from Rehoboth by the river, a city in Edom. After his death, Baal-Hanan son of Achbor succeeded him on the throne (Genesis 36:37-38).
2. He is a figure from ancient history, mentioned in the genealogical lists of the kings of Edom contemporary with the Patriarchs Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.
H7586I.origine: The name Saul means "one who is desired" or "asked for." It is a Hebrew name borne by several figures in the Bible, but this entry concerns only Saul, king of Edom, distinct from the other Sauls mentioned elsewhere in Scripture.
H7586I.emploi: Saul, king of Edom, appears four times in the Bible, only in the genealogical lists of the kings of Edom: twice in Genesis 36:37-38 and twice in the parallel of 1 Chronicles 1:48-49. These identical references show that it is the same man and the same historical period. There are no details about his life or reign: he is mentioned only for his place in the succession of Edomite kings.

sens: Levite son of Uzziah, father of Elkanah, living during the time of the divided monarchy
H7586J.detail: Saul is a Levite mentioned in the genealogy of the temple musicians during the time of the divided monarchy in Israel. He is the son of Uzziah and the father of Elkanah (1 Chronicles 6:24). This Saul, also called Joel in the same biblical passage, belongs to the priestly lineage of the Levites who served in the house of the Lord.
H7586J.origine: The name Saul means "desired" in Hebrew. Although this name is borne by several characters in the Bible — the most famous being Saul son of Kish, the first king of Israel — this Saul is a minor figure in the Levitical genealogies, simply identified by his place in the succession of ancestors.
H7586J.emploi: This Saul appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 6:24, in the genealogical list of the Levites dedicated to the service of the temple. He is a simple link in the chain of ancestors, with no particular narrative concerning him. His context is that of the organization of Levitical worship established by King David, who set up a precise structure for the musicians and the temple guards.

sens: descendants of Shaul (Saul), a man from the tribe of Simeon
H7587.detail: 1. The Saulites are the descendants of Shaul, a man from the tribe of Simeon who lived during the time of Egypt and the desert. Shaul is first mentioned in the genealogy of Simeon in Genesis 46:10, as the son of Simeon and a Canaanite woman. This name thus designates his family lineage, as is customary in Israel to identify tribal groups according to their ancestor (Numbers 26:13).
H7587.origine: The word Saulites comes from the name Shaul (שָׁאוּל), which means "asked for" or "one who has been asked for." It is a Hebrew name bearing a suffix of filiation (-ites) that marks belonging to a family or clan. The same formation is found for other Simeonite families, such as the Zerahites, descendants of Zerah.
H7587.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Numbers 26:13, in the context of the census of the Israelites in the desert after the exodus from Egypt. Moses enumerates the families of the tribe of Simeon, and the Saulites are mentioned alongside other Simeonite families such as the Zerahites, Jemuelites, Shimonites, Ohadites, and Jachinites. This genealogical enumeration served to organize the people of Israel and establish tribal responsibilities.

sens: violent and continuous noise produced by moving waters
a collection of deafening noises, cries, and confusion
crowd agitation, tumultuous disorder
massive violence and destruction
noisy manifestation of divine judgment
H7588.detail:
1. The tumult primarily refers to the crash of great waters — the powerful rumbling of a mass of water in motion. Isaiah 17:13 compares the noise of the nations "like the great waters roar": it is the image of an irrepressible and terrifying force.

2. It also refers to the confused clamor of an agitated crowd — intertwined shouts, voices rising together. Psalms 74:23 evokes "the ever-increasing tumult of those who rise against you," a gathering of noisy and threatening adversaries.

3. The word denotes the confusion of massive destruction. Psalms 40:3 speaks of the "pit of destruction" (literally "pit of tumult"), an image of an abyss of ruin. Isaiah 25:5 shows the Lord who tames "the tumult of the barbarians," putting an end to the noise of their ravage.

4. It is also the translation of God's judgment that falls: Jeremiah 25:31 states that "the noise reaches to the ends of the earth" when the Lord enters into judgment against all flesh — a crash that fills the entire world.
H7588.origine: The Hebrew word שָׁאוֹן (sha'on) comes from a root that evokes loud and powerful noise, the shockwave. It is related to words that mean "to make noise" or "to roar." The basic image is that of the rumbling of nature — the water that roars, the thunder that rumbles — before extending to all violent noise and the confusion it creates.
H7588.emploi: This word appears 16 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the prophets (Isaiah, Jeremiah) and the Psalms. It primarily characterizes terrifying natural phenomena: the roaring of waters, the rumbling of nations. But it also takes on a symbolic meaning: the tumult becomes the image of divine judgment, the fall of empires, the destruction that accompanies God's anger. In Isaiah, the tumult of the defeated peoples contrasts with the silence imposed by the Lord.
H7588.portee: This word reminds the believer that behind all the confusing and terrifying noise of the world — threats, conflicts, hostile powers — stands a God who is in control. Isaiah 25:5 says that the Lord tames the tumult of the oppressors: He is assurance that the clamor of evil is not the final word. The tumult also warns us: when God enters into judgment (Jeremiah 25:31), His action resonates to the ends of the earth.

sens: deep feeling of disdain towards something or someone
attitude of hostility mixed with hatred and contempt
deliberate insult or affront thrown in someone's face
H7589.detail:
1. Contempt is the feeling of disdain one feels towards what one judges unworthy, vile, or worthless. It is to look down on someone or something as if it does not deserve esteem. In Ezekiel 36:5, God denounces those who have seized the land of Israel "with the contempt of their soul" — they acted with a heart filled with disdain and contempt towards the people of God.
2. The word also denotes a form of active hostility: one that manifests through vengeance carried out with bitterness. Ezekiel 25:15 speaks of the Philistines who acted out of vengeance "contemptuously," meaning with a contemptuous rage, as if they were crushing something dirty under their feet.
3. Contempt can finally be an act of insult or affront: to rejoice "contemptuously" (Ezekiel 25:6) means to applaud mockingly and hatefully, to manifest one's disdain through gestures of ridicule (clapping hands, stomping feet).
H7589.origine: The Hebrew word שְׁאָט comes from a root that expresses the idea of disdain and contempt. It carries within it the image of a heart that turns away from someone with contempt, rejecting them as unworthy. The word appears mainly in poetry and prophetic texts to express the deepest feeling of rejection and hatred — not a simple critique, but a disdain that comes from the heart.
H7589.emploi: The word appears three times in the Bible, exclusively in the prophet Ezekiel (chapters 25 and 36), in the context of God's judgments against foreign nations. Ezekiel uses it to accuse the Philistines and Edom (through Ammon) of having acted with disdain and contempt towards the people and territory of Israel. In these three instances, the word is constantly associated with the idea of malice of the heart ("from the depths of the soul," "from their heart"), emphasizing that contempt is not a mere superficial feeling, but a malicious and enduring intention. That is why God promises to judge these nations: they have not only acted against Israel, but they have done so with contempt.
H7589.portee: This word reminds us that God sees not only our actions but the intentions of our hearts. Contempt is particularly grave in the eyes of God because it reveals a heart that rejects, belittles, and considers itself superior. For the reader, this invites self-examination: does he not harbor contempt towards others, disguised as judgment or mockery? At the same time, this word assures that God takes the side of those whom the nations despise: He defends the honor of His own.

sens: To treat someone with contempt, to consider them unworthy of respect
To show hostility or disdain towards a person or a people
H7590.detail:
1. To despise means to treat someone with contempt or mockery, considering them unworthy. It is an attitude of disdain that belittles the other. In Ezekiel 16:57, the daughters of the Philistines despised Jerusalem "on all sides," meaning they surrounded it with hostility and looked down upon it.
2. It also means to show enmity or contempt towards an entire people or nation. In Ezekiel 28:24-26, those who despise Israel are listed alongside those who harm her like a thorn or a bramble: contempt is a form of hostility that accompanies the intention to do harm.
H7590.origine: The Hebrew verb shat comes from a root that expresses the idea of treating poorly or looking down on. In biblical Hebrew, this verb is infrequent and appears mainly in passages concerning the attitude of enemies towards Israel or Jerusalem. The prophetic contexts of Ezekiel are its primary witnesses.
H7590.emploi: This Hebrew verb appears only three times in the Hebrew Bible, all in the book of Ezekiel. In Ezekiel 16:57, it describes how neighboring peoples (Syria, Philistines) despised Jerusalem. In Ezekiel 28:24 and 28:26, it denotes the contempt of Israel's enemies, who will be judged by God. The word always evokes a hostile and contemptuous attitude aimed at Israel or Jerusalem, often in a context of divine promise of restoration.
H7590.portee: This word reminds the Christian reader that contempt for others is an attitude that God notices and judges. The peoples who despised Israel came under divine judgment: to despise God's work towards His people is a serious error. It is an invitation to regard with respect what God values, rather than following the disdain of the world.

sens: complete destruction of a city or building
state of a collapsed and abandoned structure
loss, figurative collapse
H7591.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes the physical destruction of a city or fortification: walls are torn down, gates are broken, everything is overturned. In Isaiah 24:12, ruin is depicted alongside the devastation that strikes the city: "The broken gates are in ruins," meaning reduced to nothing, uninhabitable and barren.
2. By extension, it refers to the lamentable state of what remains: rubble, fallen stones, an empty place where life once reigned. The image is one of abandonment and death.
3. Figuratively, the word can evoke the spiritual or moral collapse of a people: when God judges, He reduces everything to nothing, like a city under siege.
H7591.origine: The Hebrew word שְׁאִיָּה (sheiyyah) comes from a root expressing the idea of desolation and emptiness. It is rare in the Bible and carries with it the visual image of ruin — the debris of a destroyed civilization. It is a grave word, laden with the threat of divine judgment upon nations.
H7591.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Isaiah 24:12. It is found in a prophetic passage where Isaiah describes the coming cosmic and political destruction: desolation spreads over the cities, the gates fall into ruin. The context is that of eschatological judgment, where God ravages the earth as punishment for sin. The word emphasizes the totality of ruin: not only destroyed but reduced to the state of abandoned remnants.
H7591.portee: This word reminds the reader that God's judgment is not a mere correction: it is a radical destruction that affects cities, kingdoms, and powers that stand against Him. For the Christian, it invites reflection on the fragility of human achievements in the face of divine holiness. Isaiah 24 announces a transfiguration of the world, and the ruin of ancient cities is its necessary prelude.

sens: To pose a question to obtain information
To request something from someone for them to give or lend it to you
To address God to know His will, to consult Him
To demand urgently, to implore
H7592.detail:
1. To pose a question: it is to inquire of someone to learn something. When Laban "asks" Rebekah about her origins (Genesis 24:47), he seeks to know who she is. The word implies a verbal exchange, a curiosity or a need to know.

2. To ask to receive: it is to pray someone to give or lend you something. The Israelites "ask" the Egyptians for gold and silver objects (Exodus 12:35), they plead with them to let them take them. It is also to borrow, as suggested by the law on lending (Exodus 22:14).

3. To consult God: it is to address the Lord, often through a priest or prophet, to know His intentions before acting. When David "consults" the Lord before battle (2 Samuel 5:23), he awaits a response that will guide him. It is an act of piety and dependence.

4. To implore urgently: it is to ask with strength and sincerity, like Agur in Proverbs (Proverbs 30:7) who "asks" for two favors from God before dying. The word then carries a note of intense supplication.
H7592.origine: This Hebrew verb comes from a root that expresses the idea of "seeking to obtain" or "seeking to know." It belongs to a family of words that all revolve around questioning and questing. In Greek, it is often translated as "aïtéo" (to ask) or "erotào" (to inquire), two verbs that also cover this range of meanings. The noun derived from it, "shéélah" (a question, a request), shows that the word describes both the act of asking a question and that of requesting something.
H7592.emploi: This verb appears 157 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the historical and wisdom books. It is first encountered in a very everyday sense: asking for news (Genesis 43:27), borrowing objects, posing practical questions. Then it takes on a major religious dimension: consulting the Lord is a central act of Israelite piety, particularly before a battle or an important decision (Judges 20:18, 1 Samuel 23:2). Samuel reports to the people "the request" for a king (1 Samuel 8:10). The word also gains a supplicatory nuance when used before God, marking a respectful dependence.
H7592.portee: This verb teaches us that asking is a fundamental attitude before God: it is to recognize that we are in need, that we do not know, and that we depend on Him. The Bible encourages the believer to consult the Lord and present their requests, not with shame, but with confidence. Asking also shows a living relationship with God, where one does not decide alone but seeks His direction. It is also a virtue towards others: knowing how to ask with respect is to recognize the other and their authority.

sens: Pose a question to obtain information
Request something, make a request
Demand, claim with authority
H7593.detail:
1. To pose a question to obtain information: this is to interrogate someone to know or learn something. When the Persian governors question the elders of the Jews about the authorization to rebuild the temple, they ask questions to understand (Ezra 5:9).
2. To request something, to make a request: this is to solicit, to pray that one is given or that something is done for them. The king orders the treasurers to deliver to Ezra "everything he asks of you," meaning all the goods he deems necessary (Ezra 7:21).
3. To demand, to claim with authority: this is to ask forcefully, as a legitimate power. When Daniel says that "no magician has demanded such a thing" from the king, he refers to the imperative order that the king imposes (Daniel 2:10).
H7593.origine: This Aramaic verb comes from a root that expresses the action of turning to someone to address them with a word, a question, or a request. It is common in biblical Aramaic, particularly in the books of Ezra and Daniel, which report exchanges between Persian authorities, wise men, and prophets.
H7593.emploi: The verb appears six times in the Hebrew Bible, only in the Aramaic portions of Ezra and Daniel. It describes three situations: first, the official interrogations of the Persian governors questioning about the rebuilding of the temple (Ezra 5:9-10); second, the requests of the Persian king to his treasurers to provide the means that Ezra claims (Ezra 7:21); finally, the demand that the king of Babylon imposes on his wise men to reveal a secret (Daniel 2:10-11, 2:27). In these three contexts, the word oscillates between cautious inquiry and authoritative command.
H7593.portee: This word shows us that asking is never neutral: it establishes a relationship of power, either in search of an answer or in exercising authority. For the believer, it reminds us that our requests to God are never orders, but a recognition that we depend on Him.

sens: Man of the Israelite community of the return from exile
H7594.detail: Scheal is an Israelite living at the time of the return from exile, under the leadership of Ezra. He appears in the list of the sons of Bani who had married foreign women and had to repudiate them according to Ezra's ordinances (Ezra 10:29). He is an ordinary member of the community who submits to the religious reform of the return.
H7594.origine: The name Scheal literally means "the one who asks" or "request" in Hebrew, formed from the root שאל (she.al, "to ask"). This root denotes the action of posing a question, soliciting, or claiming something from someone.
H7594.emploi: Scheal appears only once in the Bible, in Ezra 10:29. He is listed among the sons of Bani, a large family at the time of the return from exile. Like several other men in his community, he had married a non-Israelite woman, which was contrary to the Law. During the religious reform led by Ezra, he accepted to separate from his foreign wife to restore the religious purity of the community of Israel.

sens: A question, a request, a petition
A concrete matter that one deals with
H7595.detail:
1. The word denotes a question posed, a request or petition made to someone — what is presented to them for them to take up. In Daniel 4:17, it refers to a matter that the watchers (the angels) must report to the Most High: they are tasked with communicating something serious that He must know.
2. More broadly, it is a matter, a concrete situation that needs to be dealt with or resolved — a subject that occupies attention and requires a decision or action.
H7595.origine: It is an Aramaic word (the language spoken by the Jews in exile and which Jesus Himself spoke). It derives from the Hebrew שְׁאֵלָה (shéélah), which comes from the verb "to ask" or "to interrogate." The root evokes the idea of posing a question, making a request — something that one "raises" to someone to submit for their attention.
H7595.emploi: This word appears only once in Daniel 4:17, where it qualifies a matter that the angels must bring before God. It is an administrative or legal term: the one who receives the matter (here, the Most High) is responsible for addressing it. In this context, it refers to a serious question concerning the decree and sentence pronounced against Nebuchadnezzar.
H7595.portee: This passage reminds the reader that our most serious situations — our trials, our unanswered questions — do not go unnoticed. They are brought before God by His angels, who report on them. This is a source of encouragement: we are never alone in facing what troubles us.

sens: What one asks for, what one desires to obtain
A prayer, a supplication addressed to God
A vow, what one wishes with all their heart
A petition presented to a person of power or authority
H7596.detail:
1. The word first denotes the thing itself that one asks for, the object of the request: what one wishes to receive. In Esther 5:6, the king asks Esther: "What is your request?" — he seeks to know precisely what she desires.
2. In the context of prayer, it is the supplication addressed to God, the vow presented to Him. Hannah, the mother of Samuel, prays to the Lord earnestly, and in 1 Samuel 1:27 she says: "It was for this child that I prayed, and the Lord has granted the petition I asked of Him" — her request was to have a son.
3. In 1 Samuel 2:20, Eli speaks of "replacing" what Hannah has "lent" to the Lord: the request also becomes what is given in response, the result obtained.
4. When a person of high rank is involved, it is a solemn request: Bathsheba presents a request to David for her son Solomon (1 Kings 2:16), a petition in some sense official that a king has the power to grant or deny.
H7596.origine: The word comes from the root שׁאל (sha'al), which means "to ask, to interrogate." This root evokes the idea of posing a question or seeking something. The Hebrew word שְׁאֵלָה literally means "what is asked" or "what is inquired" — it denotes the content or object of the request itself, not the act of asking. The same root appears in words of the same family that all express this notion of request.
H7596.emploi: The word appears 14 times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in the historical books and the Psalms. In the story of Samuel, it describes Hannah's urgent prayer to God (1 Samuel 1:17, 1:27): an intimate and personal request addressed to the Lord. In the book of Esther, it takes on a more political tone: it is the request made before the king, the petition that can be granted if one has his favor (Esther 5:6-8, 7:2-3). In 1 Kings 2:16 and 2:20, Bathsheba presents her requests to King David: petitions that a queen mother can assert. Psalm 106:15 shows a nuanced sense: God grants the requests of the people, but sometimes He also sends leanness upon their soul — the word then denotes the carnal desires that Israel expresses.
H7596.portee: This word shows that prayer is not murmured timidly, but is a clear, precise request presented with confidence before God or before those who have the power to respond. Hannah prays not vaguely, but with a well-defined request: to have a child. This encourages the Christian to present their requests to the Lord with clarity and frankness, knowing that God welcomes the requests of those who sincerely seek Him. The word also shows that prayer is never just a formality: it is a real request, awaiting a real response.

sens: Man of the tribe of Judah during the time of exile and return
Son of King Jehoiachin
Father of Zerubbabel
Key figure in the restoration of the temple after the exile
H7597A.detail: 1. Schealthiel is a man of the tribe of Judah who lived during the time of the Babylonian exile and the return to the Holy Land. His name means "I have asked of God" in Hebrew, expressing the hope of a believer who prays. 2. He is the son of King Jehoiachin, also called Jeconiah, who was deported to Babylon after the fall of Jerusalem (1 Chronicles 3:17). This royal lineage makes Schealthiel a descendant of the house of David, even during the exile. 3. Schealthiel is the father of Zerubbabel, who leads the people in their return and oversees the reconstruction of the temple in Jerusalem after the exile (Ezra 3:2 and 3:8). Through him passes the continuity of the royal lineage and the fulfillment of God's promises. 4. Schealthiel plays a central role in the events of the return from exile: his son Zerubbabel receives prophetic encouragement (Haggai 1:1; Haggai 2:23) and becomes the governor of the people in the Promised Land, a symbol of restored hope.
H7597A.origine: The name Schealthiel is composed of two Hebrew elements: "shéal" (to ask, to plead) and "El" (God). It literally means "I have asked of God" or "God has heard my request." This name reflects the piety and trust in God of the one who bears it, typical of Hebrew theophoric names that proclaim a relationship with the Lord.
H7597A.emploi: Schealthiel appears six times in the Hebrew Bible, always in the books that recount the exile and return (1 Chronicles, Ezra, Nehemiah, Haggai). He is first mentioned as the son of Jehoiachin in the royal genealogy (1 Chronicles 3:17). He then becomes best known as the father of Zerubbabel, the leader of the return from exile: it is through him that the heritage of the royal house of David passes. The prophets Haggai recognize him as such, and God addresses through Zerubbabel, his son, words of promise and restoration (Haggai 1:1 and 2:23). Schealthiel thus represents the living link between the ancient royalty of Israel and the new hope of the restored people.
H7597A.portee: Schealthiel embodies the hope of the exiled people: despite captivity, the lineage of David endures, and God does not abandon His promises. His very name, "I have asked of God," encourages the reader to present their requests to the Lord with confidence, knowing that God hears and acts. Through his son Zerubbabel and the reconstruction of the temple, Schealthiel shows how God restores His people and renews His plans of love, even in the darkest moments of history.

sens: Name of a man of the tribe of Judah during the time of the Exile and the Return
Father of Zerubbabel, the governor of Judah after the Exile
H7597B.detail:
1. Schealthiel is a man of the tribe of Judah who lived during the time of the Babylonian Exile and the Return to the Promised Land. He was the son of Jehoiachin, king of Judah (or from his royal family), which made him a direct descendant of the house of David.
2. He is best known as the father of Zerubbabel, the governor of Judah who led the return of the exiles and undertook the reconstruction of the Temple. It is through Zerubbabel that Schealthiel plays a role in the history of salvation: he is mentioned three times in the book of Haggai (Haggai 1:12, 1:14, 2:2) always in relation to his son and the reconstruction of the Temple.
H7597B.origine: The name Schealthiel means "I have asked of God" or "I have requested of God." It comes from Hebrew roots expressing a request or a prayer addressed to God. This name reflects the piety of this man and the hope of his family in a context of exilic suffering.
H7597B.emploi: Schealthiel appears only in the book of Haggai, three times within three verses (1:12, 1:14, 2:2), always referred to as the father of Zerubbabel. The prophet Haggai addresses him through his son to exhort the people to get to work and rebuild the Temple. These mentions show that Schealthiel was part of the noble families returned from the Exile and that his descendants, particularly Zerubbabel, enjoyed recognized authority to lead the reconstruction project.
H7597B.portee: Schealthiel's role in biblical history reminds us that God has not abandoned His promise to the house of David, even during the Exile: the royal lineage has survived, and God is bringing it back to the Promised Land. This is a testimony to God's faithfulness to His people and the continuity of the redemptive plan through generations, despite trials.

sens: man of the tribe of Judah during the time of the Exile and the Return
father of Zerubbabel
H7598.detail: Schealthiel is an important figure in the history of Israel at the time of the return from exile to Babylon. He is a descendant of the royal house of Judah, son of Jehoiachin, the king who was formerly deported. His name means "I have asked of God" and expresses the prayer of a people awaiting deliverance. He is best known as the father of Zerubbabel, who led the reconstruction of the Temple in Jerusalem after the return from exile (Ezra 5:2).
H7598.origine: The name Schealthiel comes from Hebrew and literally means "I have asked of God." It is composed of two elements: a root expressing a request, a prayer, and the name of God (El). This name reflects the Jewish people's trust in divine goodness at a time of oppression.
H7598.emploi: Schealthiel appears only once in the Bible, in Ezra 5:2, where he is presented as the father of Zerubbabel. In this crucial historical context, after Cyrus's decree allowing the Jews to return, Zerubbabel and Joshua rise up to rebuild the Temple, supported by the prophets. Schealthiel embodies the continuity of the Davidic royal lineage despite the exile, and his existence ensures that God's promise to David regarding his descendants has been maintained even during captivity.
H7598.portee: The character of Schealthiel reminds the believer that God never forgets His people, even in exile, and that the promises made to the ancestors are fulfilled through generations. His name, "I have asked of God," invites every Christian to pray confidently in times of trial. Through him and his son Zerubbabel, God demonstrates that oppression is never final and that restoration is always possible for those who wait on Him.

sens: To be at rest, without agitation or trouble
To enjoy a deep peace, safe from danger
To live in security, without fear or oppression
To remain unchanged, stable in one's state
H7599.detail:
1. The word primarily expresses a physical and mental rest: the absence of agitation, the calm of body and mind. The freed captives are in "peace"; they no longer hear the voice of the oppressor (Job 3:18) — a tranquility regained after the trial.
2. It then designates the deep peace that comes from security: the one who listens to wisdom "will dwell in safety" and live "quietly," without fear of evil (Proverbs 1:33). It is an inner peace, the fruit of trust.
3. It can also mean enjoying rest after deliverance: Jacob "will return" and "enjoy rest and tranquility," no one will trouble him anymore (Jeremiah 30:10). It is peace regained, the absence of disturbance.
4. Finally, it expresses stability, immutability: Moab had been "quiet" since its youth, resting on its dregs, unchanged, for it was never emptied from one vessel to another (Jeremiah 48:11) — a tranquility that borders on immobility, without evolution.
H7599.origine: The Hebrew root שׁאן (sha.an) evokes the idea of resting, settling down without worry. It is related to the notion of security and stability. The word belongs to a family of expressions that describe the state of one who can finally cease fighting, who finds refuge and stability. In Hebrew, this root often expresses the contrast between agitation (flight, captivity, fear) and the cessation of all threat.
H7599.emploi: The word appears five times in the Old Testament, mainly in the books of wisdom and prophecy. It appears in Job to describe the peace of the dead freed from torment, in Proverbs as a reward for one who listens to wisdom, and several times in Jeremiah to prophesy the peaceful return of the exiled people. Its meaning varies slightly: sometimes it refers to the rest of body and heart, sometimes to the security promised by God, sometimes to immobile stability. Each use highlights an aspect of this absence of trouble: physical, emotional, or existential.
H7599.portee: This word invites the believer to understand that true peace is not the absence of fatigue, but the cessation of fear and trouble. God promises His people a deep tranquility — not immobility, but the security that allows one to live without fear. It is a word of comfort for those who suffer: tranquility will come, promised by the One who has the power to deliver from every oppressor.
